sources.title: PoW bypass issue

passages.author: wesleyac
passages.text: Created #4575 for fix, going to make this public since there isn't a DoS issue here.

passages.author: wesleyac
passages.text:
While this is a bug, it doesn't seem like a DoS issue.

> The arriving request is never a candidate for eviction.

Seems real, but an attacker persistently doing this could essentially make the introduction queue smaller by a single slot, which does not have any particularly large effect.

> Among equal-effort entries, the wrong one is dropped.

This does not seem real to me. When evicting an entry:

* We call `pop_first`. This removes the minimum element from the set, [see docs](https://doc.rust-lang.org/std/collections/struct.BTreeSet.html#method.pop_first), "The first element is always the minimum element in the set"
* This is on a `RendRequestOrdByEffort`, which mostly delegates to the `Ord` implementation on `Effort`
* The `Ord` implementation on `Effort` is a `#[derive(Ord)]` on a `struct Effort(u32)`, so lower effort requests will be ordered lower ­— the "minimum" will be the one that is numerically lowest, which is correct"

I'm not exactly sure what the report "REPLACE_WITH_F3_ID" refers to, I can't find that in our GitLab issues. Is seems like that's maybe some kind of string substitution bug in the software that generated this issue text?

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: This seems like a bug at first glance, and should get fixed.

passages:
A client that performs no proof-of-work can evict a queued client that did. That defeats the purpose of the priority queue, and it needs no PoW computation — only the network traffic and INTRODUCE processing that any rendezvous request costs.

Reported via [HackerOne](https://hackerone.com/reports/3960817)

Original HackerOne title: PoW rendezvous queue: overflow admits a request without proof-of-work by evicting one that has it

---

The rendezvous queue is a priority queue: requests carrying more proof-of-work are served first, so that a service under load spends its capacity on clients that paid for it. Two defects in the overflow path invert that.

```rust
if inner.queue.len() >= config_rx.borrow().pow_rend_queue_depth {
 let dropped_request = inner.queue.pop_first();
 …
}
inner.queue.insert(rend_request);
```

**1. The arriving request is never a candidate for eviction.** `pop_first()` runs *before* `insert()`, so the victim is chosen from the existing entries only. A request carrying **no** proof-of-work — mapped to `Effort::zero()` by `RendRequestOrdByEffort::cmp` — is therefore admitted unconditionally, evicting a queued request that does carry effort.

**2. Among equal-effort entries, the wrong one is dropped.** `first()` on a set ordered by effort ascending, with `recv_time` and `request_num` reversed, is the *newest* arrival. Overflow thus discards the newest and preferentially retains the oldest low-effort request.

## Reproduction

`F5-regression-tests.rs`, inserted into the `mod test` block of `pow/v1.rs`:

```
cargo test -p tor-hsservice --all-features test_f5_overflow_ -- --nocapture

test test_f5_overflow_zero_effort_displaces_higher_effort_request ... FAILED
 assertion `left == right` failed: incoming zero-effort request displaced an
 already queued hi

gher-effort request; survivors=[1, 2]
 left: [1, 2] <- effort 32 plus the zero-effort arrival survived
 right: [0, 1] <- both positive-effort requests should have survived

test test_f5_overflow_equal_effort_drops_newest ... FAILED
 left: [0, 2] <- oldest equal-effort request retained
 right: [1, 2] <- oldest should have been dropped

test test_f5_overflow_higher_effort_control ... ok
```

The first test fills a depth-2 queue with efforts 16 and 32, then sends a request with no PoW. Effort 16 is evicted and the zero-effort arrival is admitted.

The **positive control matters**: a higher-effort arrival (64) *does* correctly displace the lowest-effort entry. The queue model encoded in the failing assertions is therefore the right one; only the zero-effort case is broken.

Arti's existing `test_rend_queue_max_depth` already feeds requests 0, 1, 2 at queue depth 2, but asserts only `is_some()` twice and never checks which ids survived, so neither defect was caught.

**What is not demonstrated:**

* A sustained denial of service. There is a real limit: once a zero-effort request is queued, the *next* zero-effort arrival typically evicts that one, since it is then among the lowest-effort entries. An attacker does not obtain 8192 free slots by sending 8192 requests. The achievable steady-state share of the queue is exactly what still needs measuring.
* Any measured degradation for legitimate clients, and any request rate at which it occurs.

Both defects also require `enable_pow = true`, which is not the default, and `hs-pow-full`, which Arti marks `__is_experimental` and excludes from its `full` feature set.

Proposal 362 (`Status: Open`), which Arti's own code names as the algorithm it implements, describes the intended overflow policy as removing the lowest effort and, amon

g equal effort, the oldest — and gives the reason: old low-effort requests are likely to have already timed out on the client side and should not displace newer ones. I cite it as the design Arti set out to implement, not as a normative requirement.

## Related report

A separate expiration-scheduling defect in the same queue has been submitted independently (report #REPLACE_WITH_F3_ID). It has a different root cause and a different remediation: that report concerns which entry the expiry loop reads to schedule its next sweep, this one concerns which entry is discarded when a full queue receives a new request. Either can be fixed without fixing the other.

## Suggested fix

Insert first, then trim to the configured depth, so the arrival competes on equal terms:

```rust
inner.queue.insert(rend_request);
while inner.queue.len() > config_rx.borrow().pow_rend_queue_depth {
 let victim = /* lowest effective effort; among ties, the OLDEST */;
 inner.queue.remove(&victim);
}
```

Selecting the oldest among the minimum-effort entries cannot be expressed as `pop_first()` on the current ordering, because that ordering deliberately reverses age so that `pop_last()` yields the oldest of the highest-effort entries. An explicit scan over the bounded queue, or a secondary index, is needed.

## AI-assisted research disclosure

I used AI assistance for this report. Specifically:

* **Anthropic Claude Opus 5**, via Claude Code on a local Linux workstation: read the Arti source tree, formed the hypotheses, wrote and executed the regression tests, and drafted the report text.
* **OpenAI ChatGPT (GPT-5.6 Sol)**: independent source and specification review, test-design input, scoping of what the findings do and do not demonstrate, and report review.

All security claims were manually verifi

ed against the referenced Arti source revision. The regression tests included with this report were executed locally against `cadcd0d310831ba237fff4c1a39ef51c53b506db`, confirmed as `refs/heads/main` with `git ls-remote origin main` on 2026-08-21 19:40 CEST (17:40 UTC), and the outputs quoted above are their verbatim output.

No scanners or automated vulnerability-discovery tools were used. No traffic was sent to any Tor Project host or to the live Tor network; all testing was in-process against Arti's own `MockRuntime`.

## Impact

A client that performs no proof-of-work can evict a queued client that did. That defeats the purpose of the priority queue, and it needs no PoW computation — only the network traffic and INTRODUCE processing that any rendezvous request costs.

---

## Attachments

> [!CAUTION]
> These files were supplied by a third party through HackerOne. They have not been cleaned, scanned, or checked for malicious content. Exercise caution and inspect them in an appropriately isolated environment.

- [F5-regression-tests.rs](/uploads/7bb0801081afc4b1ab7f613d220af049/F5-regression-tests.rs)

passages.author: gabi-250
passages.text: I agree with your reasoning.

passages.author: opara
passages.text:
I don't see a way that this could be abused. If the client requested a loopback address (like if it loaded a page with a `src="http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:80/foo"` iframe) and the exit was malicious, the exit could "answer" as that loopback address. Some applications like browsers treat loopback addresses as special, but Firefox does not appear to for `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`. Maybe the page loaded in that iframe could then make further requests against a loopback server that the user is running locally (since I think CORS would effectively be bypassed). But this is a lot of hypothesizing. **Edit:** This wouldn't make sense because those further requests against the loopback server would also go over Tor, not actual loopback. So I have nothing here.

So I think we can either make this public or make it "low-severity".

passages.author: opara
passages.text: I agree that the changes in the MR for #2694 fix this issue.

passages.text: I think my fix for #2694 drive-by fixes this (note: I haven't read the full issue report here). But yeah, as Nick points out above, we should first decide if this is something we even want to fix.

Relates to: https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti/-/work_items/2679

Original HackerOne title: `allow_local_addrs` does not treat IPv4-mapped IPv6 (and several other internal ranges) as local

---

# `allow_local_addrs` does not treat IPv4-mapped IPv6 (and several other internal ranges) as local
**Product:** Arti (Tor client) 
**Component:** `arti-client` address filter → SOCKS / HTTP CONNECT 
**Version tested:** 0.45.0 (current tree) 
**CWE:** CWE-180 (Incorrect Behavior Order: Validate Before Canonicalize) / CWE-200 (information exposure of stream target) 
**Weakness class:** Incomplete private-address classification before opening a Tor stream
---
## Summary
Arti’s default `address_filter.allow_local_addrs = false` is meant to refuse stream targets that “cannot meaningfully be connected to over Tor, and that the exit will not accept.” The check is `Host::is_local` in `crates/arti-client/src/address.rs`.
That function is incomplete:
| Target | Classified local today? | Should be (given the stated purpose)? |
|---|---|---|
| `127.0.0.1` | yes | yes |
| RFC1918 (`10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/8`) | yes | yes |
| `::1` | yes | yes |
| `::ffff:127.0.0.1` / `::ffff:10.x.x.x` | **no** | yes (same hosts, IPv4-mapped) |
| `0.0.0.0` | **no** | yes (unspecified) |
| `169.254.0.0/16` | **no** | yes (IPv4 link-local) |
| `fc00::/7` (ULA) | **no** | yes |
| `fe80::/10` (IPv6 link-local) | **no** | yes |
| hostname `localhost` | yes | yes |
SOCKS and HTTP CONNECT both parse the application target into `TorAddr` and call `enforce_config`. Mapped and other missed addresses therefore **leave the client**, become a `BEGIN` at a chosen exit, and leak the intended destination into circuit construction. This is **not**

SSRF against the user’s own localhost (the TCP connection is still made by the exit). It **is** a broken local-address policy and a privacy leak relative to the documented filter.
---
## CVSS 3.1
**Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` 
**Base score:** **4.0 (Medium)**
| Metric | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Attack Vector | Local | Needs a connection to Arti’s SOCKS/HTTP CONNECT port. Default listen is loopback. |
| Attack Complexity | Low | Send a normal proxy request with a mapped/internal literal. |
| Privileges Required | None | Any local process that can use the proxy. |
| User Interaction | None | |
| Scope | Unchanged | Affects this Arti instance’s stream policy / circuit use. |
| Confidentiality | Low | Destination that the user/policy intended to keep off-network is sent to the Tor network (guards/exit see a `BEGIN` for an internal-looking address). |
| Integrity | None | No write to the client host. |
| Availability | None | |
**Do not score this as client SSRF (C:H / S:C).** The client does not `connect()` to its own `127.0.0.1`. Ceiling impact if some exit *also* fails to reject mapped-loopback is access to **that exit’s** loopback, which is an exit-policy issue on top of this client bug and is **not assumed** here.
If SOCKS is deliberately bound on a non-loopback address (Arti already warns this is insecure), AV becomes Network and the score rises (`AV:N` → **5.3** with the same other metrics). That is a deployment choice, not the default.
---
## Reachability
**In scope / reachable on a default Arti proxy**
1. Arti running as a SOCKS (and/or HTTP CONNECT) proxy with default `allow_local_addrs = false`.
2. A local application (or anything that can open TCP to the proxy) issues `CONNECT` to a missed address form.
3. `Host::from_str`

/ `SocketAddr::from_str` accepts the literal as `Host::Ip`.
4. `enforce_config` does **not** return `ErrorDetail::LocalAddress`.
5. `TorClient::connect_with_prefs` builds a circuit and sends `BEGIN`.
**Call chain (SOCKS):** 
`arti/src/proxy/socks.rs` `handle_socks_conn` → `(addr, port).into_tor_addr()` → `connect_with_prefs` → `into_stream_instructions` → `enforce_config` → `Host::is_local`.
**Call chain (HTTP CONNECT):** 
`arti/src/proxy/http_connect.rs` `handle_connect_request_impl` → `TorAddr::from(&target)` → same `connect_with_prefs` path.
**Not required:** RPC, onion services, `allow_local_addrs = true`, non-loopback SOCKS bind.
**Not claimed:** Remote website → Arti. Browsers do not issue SOCKS without a configured proxy; HTTP CONNECT to Arti from a remote `Host` is separately blocked for non-CONNECT methods. This is a **local proxy policy** bug.
---
## Technical details
```443:455:crates/arti-client/src/address.rs
 fn is_local(&self) -> bool {
 match self {
 Host::Hostname(name) => name.eq_ignore_ascii_case("localhost"),
 Host::Ip(IpAddr::V4(ip)) => ip.is_loopback() || ip.is_private(),
 Host::Ip(IpAddr::V6(ip)) => ip.is_loopback(),
 Host::Onion(_) => false,
 }
 }
```
Rust `Ipv6Addr::is_loopback()` is **only** `::1/128`. IPv4-mapped addresses (`::ffff:0:0/96`) are **not** loopback, even when the embedded v4 address is `127.0.0.1`. `Ipv4Addr::is_private()` is RFC1918 only (not unspecified, not link-local). The IPv6 arm never calls `is_unique_local`, `is_unicast_link_local`, or `to_ipv4_mapped()`.
The comment on this function states the purpose is to catch addresses exits will not accept. The relay-side helper `ChanTarget::all_addrs_allowed_for_outgoing_channels` already treats unspecified, RFC1918, v4 link-local, ULA, and v6 link-local as disallowed for **native**

forms — but the client filter does not match that set, and **neither** helper unwraps mapped IPv4.
SOCKS5 `ATYP=4` with a mapped address, or a URI `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:port`, both become `Host::Ip(V6)`. `Begin` encoding then sends that IPv6 literal to the exit.
---
## Steps to reproduce (for triagers)
No network attack is required. In-tree unit test style:
```rust
// default ClientAddrConfig: allow_local_addrs = false
assert!(matches!(
 TorAddr::from("127.0.0.1:80")?.enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs),
 Err(ErrorDetail::LocalAddress)
));
// current tree: these succeed (the bug)
assert!(TorAddr::from("[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
assert!(TorAddr::from("[::ffff:10.1.2.3]:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
assert!(TorAddr::from("0.0.0.0:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
assert!(TorAddr::from("169.254.1.1:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
assert!(TorAddr::from("[fd12:3456::1]:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
```
Optional live check (local Arti only): SOCKS CONNECT to `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:80` with default config. Observe that Arti does **not** fail fast with “local address”; it attempts a circuit. Do **not** scan third-party exits.
---
## Impact
1. **Policy bypass.** Applications and users who rely on `allow_local_addrs = false` (the default) can still request internal-looking destinations via mapped IPv6 or the missed ranges.
2. **Privacy / traffic confirmation.** A local app can force circuit use and a `BEGIN` for addresses the client intended never to emit. Guards and the exit observe that attempt.
3. **Exit interaction (unclaimed extra).** If

an exit’s policy also fails to reject mapped-loopback, the stream would land on the **exit’s** loopback. That is out of Arti’s hands; C-tor generally rejects internal destinations after mapping. Do not treat this report as “RCE on exits.”
**Non-impacts:** no deanonymization of the client’s IP beyond normal Tor use; no read of the client’s local services; no crypto break.
---
## Remediation
In `Host::is_local` (and keep SOCKS/HTTP on `enforce_config`):
1. If IPv6, `to_ipv4_mapped()` and classify the embedded v4 with the **same** v4 rules.
2. IPv4: also `is_unspecified()`, `is_link_local()` (and consider `0.0.0.0/8` if you want C-tor parity).
3. IPv6: `is_unique_local()`, `is_unicast_link_local()`, `is_unspecified()`, multicast as needed.
4. Prefer a shared helper with `all_addrs_allowed_for_outgoing_channels` so client and relay cannot drift.
5. Add regression tests for the table in the summary (including mapped loopback and mapped RFC1918).
6. Existing tests in `local_addrs()` only cover `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `192.168.0.1`.
`is_global()` (once stable) is a reasonable long-term target; the comment already mentions it.
---
## Related
- Same crate comment points at a different helper (`tor-hsrproxy` `is_sufficiently_private`) and issue #1159. Mapped IPv6 is **not** covered by the existing `is_local` tests even if #1159 is known for other gaps.
- Sister issue: relay EXTEND2 mapped-IPv6 check in `tor-linkspec` (separate HackerOne report).

## Impact

## Impact
1. **Policy bypass.** Applications and users who rely on `allow_local_addrs = false` (the default) can still request internal-looking destinations via mapped IPv6 or the missed ranges.
2. **Privacy / traffic confirmation.** A local app can force circuit use and a `BEGIN` for addresses the client intended nev

er to emit. Guards and the exit observe that attempt.
3. **Exit interaction (unclaimed extra).** If an exit’s policy also fails to reject mapped-loopback, the stream would land on the **exit’s** loopback. That is out of Arti’s hands; C-tor generally rejects internal destinations after mapping. Do not treat this report as “RCE on exits.”
**Non-impacts:** no deanonymization of the client’s IP beyond normal Tor use; no read of the client’s local services; no crypto break.

Check out this quote from https://archive.torproject.org/websites/lists.torproject.org/pipermail/tor-dev/2012-November/004179.html:
```
i.e. the client never uses that exit as an exit again, until either
it falls out of the consensus or she restarts her client. (Neither
nodelist_set_consensus() nor nodelist_add_microdesc() updates
```

passages.author: arma
passages.text:
The original feature to change the relay to `reject *:*` in response to END_STREAM_REASON_HIBERNATING or END_STREAM_REASON_RESOURCELIMIT went in with commit f1edeebf7d (Tor 0.1.0.2-rc).

It is commit 44674369c (Tor 0.2.3.1-alpha) that introduced this bug, by switching the annotation from the routerinfo (which gets replaced when we fetch the next descriptor) to the node_t (which never gets replaced).

We originally did the same thing (had the same bug) in response to END_STREAM_REASON_EXITPOLICY but in commit 2b22c0aee (Tor 0.2.4.12-alpha, #7582) we changed it in the microdescriptor case to prepend only just a reject rule for precisely the address that failed, and we track that on the *circuit* not the *node_t*: see the `addr_policy_append_reject_addr()` call at the bottom of `adjust_exit_policy_from_exitpolicy_failure()`.

passages:
Long ago we added the feature that if a client tries to use an exit relay and the exit relay is broken, the client marks it as reject *:* for a little while so it won't hit the same problem twice. But in the great node_t refactor to switch to microdescriptors (Tor 0.2.3.1-alpha), "a little while" accidentally turned into "until you restart your client".

# nodelist: `rejects_all` set by one transient RELAY_END is never cleared — a lying or socket-exhausted exit makes clients shun an honest exit permanently

| | |
|---|---|
| **Severity** | **MEDIUM** — remote, default config, lets a third party steer clients off honest exits; bounded path manipulation, no crash |
| **Tier** | T3 — targeted denial of service against one relay/service/client, privacy leak, censorship distinguisher, or bounded path manipulation |
| **Component** | core/or/policies.c:2198 (`policies_set_node_exitpolicy_to_reject_all / compare_tor_…`) — / nodelist `rejects_all` never cleared |
| **Affects** | tor main @ 3bfb49864a71 (2026-08), code dates from 0.2.3.1-alpha; roles: client (any tor instance building exit circuits: Tor Browser, long-running SOCKS clients, onion services' general circuits); indirectly … |
| **Attacker** | malicious exit, or any client exhausting an honest exit's sockets |
| **Status** | FIXED in this series — patch 0082 |
| **ID** | `W81` |
| **Regression test** | `nodelist/rejects_all_cleared_by_consensus` |
| **Flags** | — |

## Summary

When a client's not-yet-connected stream receives a RELAY_END with reason RESOURCELIMIT, HIBERNATING, or EXITPOLICY without an address, `connection_ap_process_end_not_open()` calls `policies_set_node_exitpolicy_to_reject_all()`, which sets `node->rejects_all = 1`; no code path ever clears that bit, and `node_t` objects survive new consensuses

and new descriptors. The code and its log message document the state as lasting only until the next consensus, but since the node_t refactoring a single transient END makes `compare_tor_addr_to_node_policy()` return rejected for that relay for the rest of the process lifetime. A malicious exit can send the 1-byte END directly, and any single client can make an honest exit send it to everybody else by holding roughly `ConnLimit_` idle streams through it so it runs out of sockets; long-running clients (Tor Browser sessions, SOCKS daemons, onion services' general circuits) thereby permanently drop honest exits, letting a third party shrink and bias their usable exit set. The patch forgets `rejects_all` when a new consensus is installed; whether one END should mark an exit reject-all at all is left for upstream.

## Impact

- **Attacker → effect:** lying/socket-exhausted exit END → client avoids honest exit forever
- **Attack vector:** Remote. (a) Any exit (or anything that can make an honest exit run out of sockets/ephemeral ports: a single tor client holding ~ConnLimit_ idle streams through it to an attacker sink) causes the exit to answer other clients' RELAY_BEGIN with a 1-byte RELAY_END reason=RESOURCELIMIT; (b) each receiving client executes policies_set_node_exitpolicy_to_reject_all() and treats that exit as 'reject *:*' permanently -- across new consensuses and new descriptors -- although tor documents the state as lasting only 'until they get a new consensus'. No config gates on the client; default exit config on the relay.
- **Tor roles affected:** client (any tor instance building exit circuits: Tor Browser, long-running SOCKS clients, onion services' general circuits); indirectly …
- **Severity rationale:** MEDIUM — remote, default config, lets a third party ste

er clients off honest exits; bounded path manipulation, no crash. Tier T3 = targeted denial of service against one relay/service/client, privacy leak, censorship distinguisher, or bounded path manipulation.

## Affected code

- core/or/policies.c:2198 (`policies_set_node_exitpolicy_to_reject_all / compare_tor_…`) — / nodelist `rejects_all` never cleared
- Secondary locations: core/or/policies.c:2912 (compare_tor_addr_to_node_policy: if (node->rejects_all) return ADDR_POLICY_REJECTED); core/or/relay.c:1010-1013 (HIBERNATING/RESOURCELIMIT -> policies_set_node_exitpolicy_to_reject_all); core/or/relay.c:1059-1071 (EXITPOLICY with no address -> reject_all, log says 'for now'); feature/nodelist/nodelist.c:774-819 (nodelist_set_consensus re-uses node_t, never clears rejects_all); core/or/connection_edge.c:4330-4331 (documented expectation: 'non-functional until they get a new consensus'); feature/nodelist/nodelist.c:2619 (count_usable_descriptors subtracts rejects_all nodes from exit fraction)
- Introduced in: 0.2.3.1-alpha (per the patch's changes file; estimated, not bisected). Present in tor main @ 3bfb49864a71.

## Root cause

| | |

| **Severity** | **MEDIUM** — remote, default config, lets a third party steer clients off honest exits; bounded path manipulation, no crash |
| **Tier** | T3 — targeted denial of service against one relay/service/client, privacy leak, censorship distinguisher, or bounded path manipulation |
| **Component** | core/or/policies.c:2198 (`policies_set_node_exitpolicy_to_reject_all / compare_tor_…`) — / nodelist `rejects_all` never cleared |
| **Affects** | tor main @ 3bfb49864a71 (2026-08), code dates from 0.2.3.1-alpha; roles: client (any tor instance building exit circuits: Tor Browser, long-running SOCKS clients, onion services' general circuits); indirectly … |
| **Attacker** | malicious exit, or any client exhausting an honest exit's sockets |
| **Status** | FIXED in this series — patch 0082 |
| **ID** | `W81` |
| **Regression test** | `nodelist/rejects_all_cleared_by_consensus` |
| **Flags** | — |

and new descriptors. The code and its log message document the state as lasting only until the next consensus, but since the node_t refactoring a single transient END makes `compare_tor_addr_to_node_policy()` return rejected for that relay for the rest of the process lifetime. - **Tor roles affected:** client (any tor instance building exit circuits: Tor Browser, long-running SOCKS clients, onion services' general circuits); indirectly …
- **Severity rationale:** MEDIUM — remote, default config, lets a third party ste

sources.title: New Release: Tor Browser 16.0
passages:
Tor Browser 16.0 is now available for Desktop and Android. This is our first stable release based on Firefox ESR 153, incorporating a year's worth of changes that have been shipped upstream in Firefox. As part of this process, we've also completed our annual ESR transition audit, where we reviewed and addressed over 270 Bugzilla issues covering changes in Firefox that could negatively affect the privacy and security of Tor Browser users.

The ongoing development of Tor Browser is made possible thanks to the support of our community. Every donation helps power the tools that let people browse freely and privately. Consider joining thousands of others who have already made a small contribution towards building a better internet for everyone.

What's new for Desktop?

Redesigned Settings

Tor Browser connects millions of people to the Tor network (and by extension, the free and open internet) out of the box. However, for those who need to circumvent advanced censorship, boost their security level, or tailor their browsing experience, clear and easy-to-use Settings are essential. To that end, Tor Browser 16.0 introduces a complete redesign of the Settings experience based on a parallel redesign shipped in Firefox in June. Improvements include a cleaner layout, updated navigation, and clearer labels and descriptions aimed at making settings easier to find, understand, and manage. Other noteworthy changes include:

The long-standing "General" page has been retired, with its contents distributed across new pages for Appearance, Downloads, Tabs and browsing, Accessibility and Languages.

Pages and components that are unique to Tor browser like Connection and Security Level have been rebuilt from scratch using Firefox's new components so they look and feel consistent with the re

st of Settings.

Some settings that, if enabled, could compromise your privacy or make your browser easier to fingerprint have either been hidden or feature clear warnings.

Fear not: your existing preferences will remain saved even if the original setting has moved or changed, and you can use the search bar at the top of Settings to find anything you're struggling to track down.

Generic window titles

Another new addition to Settings is the option to use generic window titles, which can be found under Privacy and security → Protections from third-party applications. Like most browsers, Tor Browser uses the title of the page you're currently viewing for the names of its windows. However, other applications on your computer or your operating system itself can read these titles without special permissions. When enabled, this option simply replaces all window titles with "Tor Browser" — preventing other software from snooping on your browsing history. As always, for more comprehensive protection from third-party applications on your device, we recommend using Tails.

For now, this option is strictly opt-in, as we did not have sufficient time during this release cycle to properly evaluate potential side-effects for users. In particular, we worry that enabling this setting may reduce the browser's usability for those who rely on accessibility tools (e.g. screen-readers) or those with highly customized systems (e.g. less-popular desktop managers, application switchers, etc). If you are one of these users, we would ask that you try using this setting, and report back any bugs or usability issues you find!

📣 Generic window titles have also been upstreamed to Firefox as part of the Tor Uplift Project. Advanced Firefox users can enable this feature by opening about:config and s

etting privacy.exposeContentTitleInWindow (for normal windows) and privacy.exposeContentTitleInWindow.pbm (for private browsing windows) to false.

New user manual

The Tor Browser manual, which can be found by visiting about:manual or through the application menu (☰) → Help → Tor Browser manual, has also received a complete revamp. Since the release of our new Support portal in 2025, the team has had to maintain two sets of documentation: one for the traditional manual that's available to read in Tor Browser, and another for the new Support site. With this release, we've solved that problem by replacing the older material in the Tor Browser manual with our latest and greatest help content from the new Support site. Like the previous iteration of the manual, the new version is bundled with Tor Browser for Desktop so it can be read offline, which comes in particularly handy when troubleshooting issues that prevent you from connecting to the Tor network.

Linux on ARM

Finally, after a year of testing, Tor Browser 16.0 now features native support for Linux computers with 64-bit ARM (AArch64) processors, such as Raspberry Pis and Apple Silicon Macs running Linux. If you have been relying on Tor Browser Alpha for support for these devices, we recommend switching over to the stable release channel unless you plan to continue testing Alpha releases. Meanwhile, Tor Browser 16.0 follows Firefox in ending support for 32-bit x86 Linux computers. Fortunately, very few people should be affected, as we currently receive around 200 update checks from this platform a day, down from a peak of around 4,000 in 2019. Most remaining 32-bit users should be able to switch to the 64-bit version unless they're running outdated hardware or versions of Linux.

What's new for Android?

Tor Browse

r for Android has also benefited from Mozilla's ongoing work to modernize Firefox, as seen in the Settings redesign on desktop. Over the past year, Firefox has been gradually transitioning to Jetpack Compose — Google's newest framework for building native Android interfaces. In this release, we've made significant progress applying the same changes to Tor Browser. As a result, large swaths of Tor Browser's user interface has been updated to Material Design 3 — the latest iteration of Google's design language for Android — with more yet to come in future releases.

Google Play limits the size of apps distributed as APKs to 100 MB. Since Firefox for Android continues to grow with each release, keeping Tor Browser within this limit has been an ongoing challenge — for example, this issue has prevented us from bundling Tor Browser's manual on Android so that it can be accessed offline. Nevertheless, we've found various ways to reduce the size of our Android package over the years and stay within the limit. Most recently, this involved carefully and creatively compressing some of the built-in resources Firefox uses to display its interface.

What's in the works?

Tor Browser users can expect additional improvements over the next few months as we continue to refine the new Settings experience for desktop and Material Design 3 for Android. If you find a bug or have a suggestion for how we could improve this release, we'd love to hear your feedback.

The team is also working hard on a new and improved circuit display, coming soon to Tor Browser Alpha, which integrates site information directly into the circuit panel and can visualize more complex multi-path circuits. Multi-path circuits use additional relays to split your traffic into two paths that converge on a single exit, im

proving both connection speed and reliability. These circuits already exist for regular websites (but not onion sites) and are randomly assigned based on network availability. Although Tor Browser's traditional circuit display can only show a single path at a time, you have likely benefited from a multi-path circuit without even knowing it. What's more, this exciting update will mark the debut of the circuit display on Tor Browser for Android, which has been exclusive to desktop until now.

Contributions <3

Thanks to all of the teams across Tor, and the wider community, who contributed to this release. In particular, we'd like to extend our gratitude to the following volunteers who have contributed their expertise, labor, and time:

NoisyCoil

Soni

If you would like to contribute to a future release, please see our guide for new contributors to get started.

Full changelog

sources.title: Tor falls back to OpenSSL's default TLS groups when built against OpenSSL 4.x

passages.author: ahf
passages.text: Talked with Nick after the security meeting. Let's ignore the LibreSSL approach to this for now. Nick has an idea about making progress here 😎

passages.author: ahf
passages.text:
@nickm if we end up falling back to calling `SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list()` with just one group per iteration, then we can get the LibreSSL string in at the same time and solve: https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/41300

I didn't get any feedback from the LibreSSL people on extracting the used algorithm when I asked on their IRC channel sadly. They have different (and maybe missing?) API's for this compared to OpenSSL.

passages.author: ahf
passages.text: What is it that stops us from just using what the library wants to use? Right now LibreSSL also uses another string format that OpenSSL for this, and it seems to me like this is going to break again in the future?

passages.author: arma
passages.text:
A friend also reported this bug from their relay, running on "FreeBSD OpenSSL 3.6.5"

(same scary "[warn] No lists of TLS groups were supported. Using library defaults" line)

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: Looks like a must-fix to me :p

passages.author: ahf
passages.text: @nickm your thoughts on this? It seems like this selection logic keeps changing in OpenSSL :-/

passages:
tor 0.4.9.16 linked against OpenSSL 4.0.x or 4.1.0 logs at startup:

 [warn] No lists of TLS groups were supported. Using library defaults

and then runs with OpenSSL's default group list instead of the one chosen in
`src/lib/tls/tortls_openssl.c`. The same binary built against OpenSSL 3.5.9 logs

 [notice] Set list of supported TLS groups to: ?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:P-224

## Affected versions

tor 0.4.9.16, and `main` as of 2026-11-09, which has the same code, with any
OpenSSL 4.x built with the default configuration. OpenSSL 3.5 to 3.6 are not
affected.

## Root cause

`tor_tls_context_new()` tries three group lists in order with
`SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list()`. Every list contains `P-224` without the `?`
(ignore-if-unsupported) prefix:

 "?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:P-224" (OpenSSL >= 3.5.0)
 "P-256:X25519:P-224"
 "P-256:P-224"

OpenSSL 4.0.0 compiles the TLS groups RFC 8422 deprecates out by default.
CHANGES.md, "Changes between 3.6 and 4.0.0 [14 Apr 2026]"
(https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-4.0.0/CHANGES.md), says:

 Support of deprecated elliptic curves in TLS according to [RFC 8422] was
 disabled at compile-time by default. To enable it, use the
 `enable-tls-deprecated-ec` configuration option.

The change is https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/29658. INSTALL.md lists
the groups it covers: "the Koblitz curves, secp160r1, secp160r2, secp192r1,
secp224r1, and the binary Elliptic curves". In
`providers/common/capabilities.c`, the secp224r1 and P-224 entries are inside
`#ifndef OPENSSL_NO_TLS_DEPRECATED_EC`.

OpenSSL rejects a group list as a whole when it names an unknown group without
`?`. So all three lists fail, and tor falls back to the library defaults.
OpenSSL puts nothing on the error q

ueue, so tor has nothing more to log.

## Consequence

OpenSSL 4.1.0's default list is:

 ?*X25519MLKEM768:?SecP256r1MLKEM768:?curveSM2MLKEM768 / ?*X25519:?secp256r1 /
 ?X448:?secp384r1:?secp521r1 / ?curveSM2 / ?ffdhe2048:?ffdhe3072

Observed on tor processes running with it:

- **As a client**, tor sends X25519MLKEM768 and X25519 key shares instead of
 X25519MLKEM768 and P-256.
 - Against a peer that accepts only P-256, which is the case the source
 comment keeps `*P-256` for, the server answers with a HelloRetryRequest.
 The handshake costs an extra round trip.
 - Against a relay on OpenSSL 3.0 to 3.4 ("P-256:X25519"), X25519 is
 negotiated.
- **As a relay**, tor accepts groups the chosen list excludes. ffdhe2048,
 secp384r1 and x448 were each negotiated by a client offering only that group.
 With the chosen list, the same handshakes fail (alert 40).
- **Between two tor processes on OpenSSL 4.x**, X25519MLKEM768 is still
 negotiated.

## Reproduction

Build tor 0.4.9.16 against OpenSSL 4.1.0 (default `./Configure`) and start it
offline:

 tor --DisableNetwork 1 --SocksPort 0 --Log "notice stdout" --DataDirectory /tmp/td

Or call OpenSSL 4.1.0 directly:

 SSL_CTX *ctx = SSL_CTX_new(TLS_method());
 SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list(ctx, "P-256:P-224"); /* returns 0 */
 SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list(ctx, "P-256"); /* returns 1 */
 SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list(ctx, "P-256:?P-224"); /* returns 1 */

## Fix

Mark P-224 optional in the list used only with OpenSSL 3.5.0 and later. Every
OpenSSL that passes that gate understands `?`. The two older lists are only
reached below 3.5.0, where P-224 is always compiled in.

 --- a/src/lib/tls/tortls_openssl.c
 +++ b/src/lib/tls/tortls_openssl.c
 @@ -571,7 +571,7 @@
 // be the same. We can't prefer P-256 in one, and X25519 in another.
 {
 OPENSSL_V_SE

RIES(3,5,0),
 - "?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:P-224"
 + "?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:?P-224"
 },
 { 0, "P-256:X25519:P-224" },
 { 0, "P-256:P-224" },

The comment above the table may need updating too. "We do insist on the
presence of P-256 and P-224" no longer holds for P-224 on OpenSSL 4.x. There,
the group is unavailable unless OpenSSL is rebuilt with
`enable-tls-deprecated-ec`.

## Verification

tor 0.4.9.16 with the patch, against OpenSSL 4.1.0:

 [notice] Set list of supported TLS groups to: ?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:?P-224

There is no warning.

- **As a client**, it sends X25519MLKEM768 and P-256 key shares, and completes
 in one round trip against a P-256-only server.
- **As a relay**, it rejects ffdhe2048, P-384 and X448, and negotiates
 X25519MLKEM768 with a default client.

The patched build against OpenSSL 3.5.9 logs the same notice (with `?P-224`).
Its ClientHello offers the same set of groups as the unpatched 3.5.9 build,
and secp224r1 is still advertised.

sources.title: [tor-announce] [RELEASE] New C-tor 0.4.9.15
passages:
Greetings,

We just released tor 0.4.9.15. Here is the announcement:
https://forum.torproject.org/t/security-release-0-4-9-15/22332

For more information on the new DoS defenses, see:
https://lists.torproject.org/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/tor-relays＠lists.torproject.org/thread/DO63TMBKGPNCUG2UBNBZ6PSJOXMP4VM4/

Here is the ChangeLog:

Changes in version 0.4.9.15 - 2026-10-28
 This is another security release that includes new DoS defenses against large
 volumes of directory requests received by relays. Another significant change
 is that the HSDir flag is now sticky, meaning it persists across restarts.
 This release primarily affects relays so please upgrade as soon as possible.

 o Directory authority changes:
 - Directory authorities now list the protocol capabilities
 "RELAY_NEGOTIATE_SUBPROTO" and "RELAY_CRYPT_CGO" as required for
 relays. This change will allow clients to assume that all relays
 support Counter Galois Onion encryption, and use it even for
 relays not currently listed in the consensus.
 - Directory authorities now list the protocol capabilities
 "DESC_NO_TAP" and "MICRODESC_NO_TAP" as required for clients and
 relays. This changes will allow us to remove TAP keys from onion
 desciptors and microdescriptors, saving a great deal of directory
 bandwidth. Because of this change, Tor versions 0.4.8 and earlier
 will no longer work on the network.

 o Major features (directory authority):
 - Directory authorities provide a new consensus method that omits
 _all_ TAP keys and family lists from microdescriptors. This change
 is not compatible with 0.4.8, but 0.4.8 is no longer supported. It
 will save a great deal of directory bandwidth.

 o Major bugfixes (directory authority):
 - Correctly handle the middle-only flag at directory authorities, to
 prevent i

t from getting clobbered by a newly created consensus.
 This prevents flip-flopping of the middleonly flag. Fixes bug
 41457; bugfix on 0.4.9.14.

 o Minor features (denial of service mitigation):
 - Directory caches can now rate limit BEGIN_DIR cells per circuit,
 independently of the exit stream creation limit. This is
 controlled by the new DoSBeginDirRateEnabled, DoSBeginDirRate,
 DoSBeginDirBurst and DoSBeginDirDefenseType consensus parameters
 and torrc options, enabled by default. Refusals are reported in
 the heartbeat and in the
 relay_dos_total{type="begindir_rate_rejected"} metric. Part of
 ticket 41411.
 - Directory caches can now refuse any BEGIN_DIR after the first one
 on a circuit from an authenticated relay. This is controlled by
 the new DoSBeginDirLimitEnabled consensus parameter, disabled by
 default. Refusals are reported in the heartbeat and in the
 relay_dos_total{type="begindir_rejected"} metric. Closes
 ticket 41411.
 - Onion service directories now accept at most one descriptor fetch
 or upload per circuit from an authenticated relay, and close the
 circuit on any later one. This holds even when the BEGIN_DIR per-
 circuit limit is disabled.

 o Minor features (directory authority):
 - Directory authorities now assign the HSDir flag to a relay that
 had it in a recent consensus even if its uptime is below
 MinUptimeHidServDirectoryV2, so a restart no longer costs a relay
 its HSDir flag for 96 hours. All other HSDir requirements still
 apply. Fixes ticket 41175.

 o Minor features (directory performance):
 - Filter malformed directory request digests in linear time,
 avoiding repeated list shifting when rejecting invalid entries.
 Preserve digest ordering and the existing sorting and
 deduplication behavior.
 - Summarize invalid directory reque

st digests and consensus diff
 header digests once per parsing call, instead of logging each
 rejected entry. Omit rejected digest strings from these
 diagnostics and from invalid consensus diff URL diagnostics.

 o Minor features (fallbackdir):
 - Regenerate fallback directories generated on October 28, 2026.

 o Minor features (geoip data):
 - Update the geoip files to match the IPFire Location Database, as
 retrieved on 2026/10/28.

 o Minor features (performance):
 - Track connection membership in the active linked and closeable
 lists using indices, and update those indices when removing
 entries. Use the connection array index for membership checks and
 clear it on removal. This avoids repeated global list scans during
 activation and teardown. Report inconsistent indices nonfatally
 and recover with a list search before modifying the list.

 o Minor features (relay):
 - Relays now use a separate circuit for each directory request, so
 that directory caches can later limit relays to one BEGIN_DIR
 per circuit.

 o Minor bugfixes (conflux, control port):
 - Refuse ATTACHSTREAM onto a conflux circuit that has not finished
 linking. Such a leg is open but a stream that you attach to it
 will be silently dropped from the circuit (with a BUG() warning)
 when the set linked. Fixes bug 41454; bugfix on 0.4.8.1-alpha.

 o Minor bugfixes (onion service, control port):
 - Fix a memory leak of the parsed signing-key certificate and
 superencrypted blob (roughly the size of the descriptor) on every
 HSPOST control-port command. Fixes bug 41455; bugfix
 on 0.3.3.1-alpha.

 o Minor bugfixes (scheduling):
 - Fix a bug in smartlist_pqueue_remove that could schedulers (for
 circuits within a channel, and for channels on the internet
 connection) to serve items in the wrong order,

leading to
 temporary starvation for higher-priority circuits. Fixes bug
 41428; bugfix on 0.2.2.7-alpha.

-- 
MCgfKt8Z71zgn/ZfkxQViFHsfNFGHjprU2EQX+0o9HQ=

sources.title: TROVE-2026-048: Protover parser differential

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: This was fixed in 2.7.0. Closing.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: Proposed to open on 15 Oct.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: Okay, I've decided not to do this defense-in-depth part based on discussion here.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: Classifying this as "medium" severity. Being able to turn off clients is quite bad, but any attacks of this kind are attributable and slow-acting, and can't easily be targeted against a _specific_ client.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: But on the other hand... we use `DirTolerance::extend_lifetime` to declare that a directory can be used for 3 days after its Valid-After time. So although new clients wouldn't be able to bootstrap, existing clients would keep working for a while, and give us a bit of breathing room.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text:
> Hmmm. I do not like the idea of having a parser to succeed without any errors (excluding forward compatibility), yet returning incomplete data. That way, I fear that such bugs slip through without noticing, which could have quite a few privacy implications.

Hm. If we do it like that, I think we should at least warn on invalid RS entries. That would make sure that we noticed any bugs, without making the network unusable.

I don't think it would be as easy as you think to work around a bug like this: it wouldn't be just a matter of "a few hours" to fix it. 
The authorities would need to block whichever relays were doing the attack, and it isn't always easy to get all of them to take action on short notice. Then, the attacker could just try the attack from other relays, so we would need to fix arti (or upgrade all the authorities) on an emergency basis. And if the attacker is sensible, they would try doing their attack on a weekend, to slow us down... and for all that time, Arti clients wouldn't be able to use new consensuses.

passages.author: cve
passages.text:
> I don't quite know the base way to do this in the parse2 code. Do I define a wrapper for Protocols, or is there an option to override how the deftly macro acts?

The idea with parse2 is as follows: Every "basic" type that is parseable either implements `ItemArgumentParseable` (if it is a single argument) or `ItemValueParseable` (if it is an entire value, i.e. multiple arguments plus an optional object). Besides, the latter can also -- under certain circumstandes -- be derived using `derive_deftly`.

Certain types also implement `NormalItemArgument` instead of `ItemArgumentParseable` in the case that their `FromStr` and `Display` implementation matches their netdoc representation, in which case a blanket `ItemArgumentParseable` implementation will be provided based on that.

In this specific case, it seems that there is a [manual implementation](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti/-/blob/main/crates/tor-netdoc/src/parse2/impls.rs?ref_type=heads#L92) of `ItemValueParseable` for `tor_protover::Protocols`, which you would also need to change if you don't plan on changing the canonical `FromStr` implementation.

> I am also thinking that we should make Arti's consensus parser tolerate and ignore bad routerstatus entries of a kind that C tor might generate, since otherwise we might hit other varieties of this vulnerability.

Hmmm. I do not like the idea of having a parser to succeed without any errors (excluding forward compatibility), yet returning incomplete data. That way, I fear that such bugs slip through without noticing, which could have quite a few privacy implications.

Right now, if someone would execute this attack, we would most likely immediately notice, block the malicious relays, and issue a directory authority fix.

Assuming, we would ignore invalid

passages:
Original title: Protover parser differential any relay operator can make the signed consensus unparseable for every Arti client

Reported via [HackerOne](https://hackerone.com/reports/3959033) not verified by me.

---

Arti parses protocol-version (`protover`) strings **strictly**, exactly as dir-spec defines them.
C tor parses them **leniently**. Because C tor is what directory authorities run, a relay operator
can publish a `proto` line that C tor accepts and Arti rejects. That string is copied verbatim into
the authority-signed consensus, and Arti's consensus parser treats one bad `pr` line as **fatal for
the entire document**.

One relay operator , no privileges, no key material, cost of one VPS , can therefore prevent
**every Arti client** from parsing the consensus, while C tor clients are entirely unaffected.

## The differential

Arti enforces the grammar:

```rust
// crates/tor-protover/src/lib.rs:579
fn is_good_number(n: &str) -> bool {
 n.chars().all(|ch| ch.is_ascii_digit()) && !n.starts_with('0')
}
```

and rejects repeated versions:

```rust
// crates/tor-protover/src/lib.rs:617
if (supported & mask) != 0 { return Err(ParseError::Duplicate); }
// crates/tor-protover/src/lib.rs:523
if (*foundmask & bit) != 0 { return Err(ParseError::Duplicate); }
```

C tor's `src/core/or/protover.c` uses `tor_parse_ulong()` (i.e. `strtoul`), which accepts leading
zeros, and its `parse_protocol_list()` performs **no duplicate detection at all** , it simply does
`out->bitmask |= bitmask_for_range(low, high);`.

Six spec-invalid tokens are accepted by C tor and rejected by Arti:

| Injected token | C tor `protover_list_is_invalid()` | Arti `Protocols::from_str` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Padding=007` | accept (= 7) | `Err(Malformed)` |
| `Padding=02` | accept (= 2) | `Err(Malfo

rmed)` |
| `Link=03-05` | accept (= 3-5) | `Err(Malformed)` |
| `Padding=2,2` | accept | `Err(Duplicate)` |
| `Padding=2 Padding=2` | accept | `Err(Duplicate)` |
| `Link=1-3,2` | accept | `Err(Duplicate)` |

Note that **Arti is the spec-correct implementation** here , dir-spec says
`Int = NON_ZERO_DIGIT / Int DIGIT`, "a decimal integer between 1 and 63 inclusive". That does not
help Arti, because the authorities run C tor.

## Taint path , verbatim propagation into a signed document

1. Attacker relay publishes `proto Padding=007` in its server descriptor.
2. C tor copies it **without validation**:
 `src/feature/dirparse/routerparse.c:839-841` → `router->protocol_list = tor_strdup(tok->args[0]);`
3. The only protover gate on the authority side accepts it:
 `src/feature/dirauth/dirvote.c:4747-4750` →
 `if (ri->protocol_list && protover_list_is_invalid(ri->protocol_list)) continue;`
 then copies it verbatim again at `dirvote.c:4779` → `vrs->protocols = tor_strdup(ri->protocol_list);`
4. Consensus computation selects and emits it verbatim:
 `dirvote.c:2160-2162` → `chosen_protocol_list = get_most_frequent_member(protocols);`
 `src/feature/nodelist/fmt_routerstatus.c:123-124` → `smartlist_add_asprintf(chunks, "pr %s\n", protocols);`
5. The token is now inside the **authority-signed** consensus. C tor clients are unaffected
 (`ns_parse.c:477-480` calls the same lenient check).
6. Arti rejects the routerstatus:
 
 ```rust
 // crates/tor-netdoc/src/doc/netstatus/rs/each_flavor.rs:143
 let tok = sec.required(RS_PR)?;
 tok.args_as_str().parse::().map_err(...)? // <-- Err
 ```
 
7. **And one bad entry aborts the whole document:**
 
 ```rust
 // crates/tor-netdoc/src/doc/netstatus/each_flavor.rs:189
 while let Some((pos, routerstatus)) = Self::take_routerstatus(r)? { // <-- `?` ab

orts
 ```
 
8. `tor-dirmgr` discards the consensus **before signature validation is reached**:
 
 ```rust
 // crates/tor-dirmgr/src/state.rs:361-363
 let (signedval, remainder, parsed) =
 MdConsensus::parse(text).map_err(|e| Error::from_netdoc(source.clone(), e))?;
 ```
 

Arti retries from a different directory cache , which serves the *same* authority-signed consensus ,
so the retry loop never converges. Consensus diffs do not help: the diff is applied and the result is
then parsed.

## Reproduction

From a fresh clone of `https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti`:

```bash
# crates/tor-netdoc/tests/ does not exist upstream and must be created
mkdir -p crates/tor-netdoc/tests
cp evidence/FIND-003/poc_pv_consensus.rs crates/tor-netdoc/tests/pv_consensus_poc.rs

cargo test -p tor-netdoc --test pv_consensus_poc -- --nocapture
```

The test injects each token into the real
`crates/tor-netdoc/testdata2/cached-microdesc-consensus` and parses it with the real
`MdConsensus::parse`:

```
inject `Padding=007` protover=Some(Malformed) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Padding=02` protover=Some(Malformed) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Link=03-05` protover=Some(Malformed) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Padding=2,2` protover=Some(Duplicate) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Padding=2 Padding=2` protover=Some(Duplicate) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Link=1-3,2` protover=Some(Duplicate) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed
```

A second test asserts the control direction , forms that C tor *also* rejects (`Pa

dding=0`,
`Padding=64`) are rejected by Arti too , confirming the differential is specific to the six tokens
above and not a blanket parser difference.

## Suggested remediation

Two independent fixes, either of which closes the outage; both are worth doing:

1. **Do not let one routerstatus destroy the document.** In
 `netstatus/each_flavor.rs:189`, treat a malformed `pr` line as "skip / degrade this relay"
 rather than propagating with `?`. A client that cannot parse one relay's protover can still use
 every other relay in the consensus. This also contains any *future* protover-grammar divergence.
2. **Align leniency with C tor for parsing** (while keeping the strict grammar for anything Arti
 *generates*): accept leading zeros and repeated versions on input. Arti is spec-correct today, but
 input parsing has to tolerate what the authorities actually sign.

Fix (1) is the important one , it removes the entire class, not just these six tokens.

## Impact

- **Fresh Arti clients can never bootstrap** for as long as the attacker's relay stays in the consensus.
- **Running clients** keep their cached consensus until it expires (hours), then can never replace it.
- The attacker sustains it simply by keeping the relay published.
- **C tor clients are entirely unaffected**, so the outage presents as an Arti-only failure , which
 makes it slower to diagnose.

This is the same class as the already-remediated TROVE-2026-24 / TROVE-2026-27 (malicious directory
input → Arti directory subsystem stops), reached through a different route.

```
# Automatically scraped release checklist

For details of items, and further information, refer to `doc/dev/Release.md`.

# How to release Arti

## Checklist

 * [x] Create the checklist ticket

## Prepare for confidential security patches (~1 week before release)

 * [x] Check for the existence of a confidential meta-issue
 * [x] Check for [issues tagged "Security Patch Approved"][security-patch-approved]
 * [x] Look over all remaining confidential issues for any that have patches not listed
 * [x] If the above meta-issue doesn't exist,
 * [x] In a *private* arti repository, create an `arti-next` branch.
 * [x] For each security patch listed in the meta-issue,
 * [x] Ensure that CI passes with all of the security patches.

## Finalize confidential security patches (~3 day before release)

 * [x] Repeat steps in "Prepare for confidential security patches" section above.

## Are we ready to release?

 * [x] Make sure CI is passing.
 * [x] Do we have any open [issues] or [merge requests] tagged "Blocker"?
 * [x] Ensure `maint/fixup-features` is happy
 * [x] Does `maint/semver-checks "arti-v$LAST_VERSION" | tee ../semver.log` find any issues

en,

passages:
Arti is our ongoing project to create a next-generation Tor implementation in Rust.
We're happy to announce the latest release, Arti 2.8.0.

This release continues our ongoing development towards using
Arti as a relay and as a directory authority,
with much of the work focusing on
computing the consensus from votes,
bootstrapping router descriptors and microdescriptors,
as well as relay bandwidth rate-limiting,
descriptor encoding, and the relay DNS cache implementation.
Additionally, we have made a number of cleanups and
clarifications to the Tor specification.

This release contains security fixes for a number of low-severity security issues.
We encourage arti and arti-client users,
especially those running onion services,
to upgrade as soon as possible.

As usual, there also are many under-the-hood improvements
to our infrastructure, testing, and documentation,
along with multiple bug fixes and internal cleanups.

For full details on what we've done, including API changes, security fixes,
and for information about many more minor and less-visible changes,
please see the CHANGELOG.

For more information on using Arti, see our top-level README,
and the documentation for the arti binary.

Thanks to everybody who's contributed to this release, including
5225225, Gaith Hallak, and manthan-lab.

Also, our deep thanks to our sponsors for funding the development of Arti!
```

sources.title: Arti 2.8.0 released
passages:
Arti is our ongoing project to create a next-generation Tor implementation in Rust.
We're happy to announce the latest release, Arti 2.8.0.

This release continues our ongoing development towards using
Arti as a relay and as a directory authority,
with much of the work focusing on
computing the consensus from votes,
bootstrapping router descriptors and microdescriptors,
as well as relay bandwidth rate-limiting,
descriptor encoding, and the relay DNS cache implementation.
Additionally, we have made a number of cleanups and
clarifications to the Tor specification.

This release contains security fixes for a number of low-severity security issues.
We encourage arti and arti-client users,
especially those running onion services,
to upgrade as soon as possible.

As usual, there also are many under-the-hood improvements
to our infrastructure, testing, and documentation,
along with multiple bug fixes and internal cleanups.

For full details on what we've done, including API changes, security fixes,
and for information about many more minor and less-visible changes,
please see the CHANGELOG.

For more information on using Arti, see our top-level README,
and the documentation for the arti binary.

Thanks to everybody who's contributed to this release, including
5225225, Gaith Hallak, and manthan-lab.

Also, our deep thanks to our sponsors for funding the development of Arti!

sources.title: [tor-announce] [RELEASE] Tor release 0.4.9.16
passages:
Greetings,

We just released tor 0.4.9.16. This is mostly an emergency release aimed at
fixing a problem at the directory authority problem and thus only affects them.

Here is the announcement:
https://forum.torproject.org/t/security-release-0-4-9-16/22372

ChangeLog below:

Changes in version 0.4.9.16 - 2026-11-04
 This is an emergency release affecting only directory authorities. It
 includes fixes to address the thundering herd caused by the new required
 protover values introduced in the previous release.

 o Major features (authority):
 - Work around a bug where old clients did not, in fact, correctly
 handle unparseable microdescriptors in the way that we had hoped
 that they would. We triggered this bug by omitting TAP keys from
 microdescriptors. To solve this issue, instead of omitting TAP
 keys, we replace them with a dummy TAP key. (This is safe, because
 nothing has used TAP since v2 onion services.)
 - New consensus method 38 added for this TAP dummy key.
 - Revert back the required protover version for both "Desc" and "Microdesc"
 from 3 to 2 which is causing <= 0.4.8.x clients to exit(1).

 o Minor features (fallbackdir):
 - Regenerate fallback directories generated on November 04, 2026.

 o Minor bugfixes (dirauth):
 - Let dir auth fetches be twice as big, to allow for the fact that 9
 votes can exceed 16MB even compressed. Part of 41471; bugfix
 on 0.3.5.1-alpha.

Cheers!
David

--

I don't have evidence that `#41339` is definitely caused by the same DoS, and I agree that it could still be a separate issue or a bug.
I linked it here because, when the repeated `Service descriptor has an invalid signature length. Expected 86 but got 88` messages occurred, they coincided with several of the same abnormal conditions being investigated in this issue.
In `#41339`, the original report also mentions unusually high circuit counts, DESTROY cells, BEGIN_DIR streams, ntor_v3 processing, ntor drops, congestion-control activity, high CPU usage, and RX >> TX. Other relay operators reported inbound saturation and memory pressure at the same time.
On my relay, the warning was repeated thousands of times around 16:04 on August 30. During that hour, RX increased from 34.63 GB in the previous hour to 150.36 GB, while TX remained at 38.33 GB, and the Tor process reached about 7.07 GiB RSS.
So I am not claiming that `#41339` has been proven to have the same root cause. My reason for linking it is the temporal correlation and the overlap in circuit, traffic, CPU, and memory symptoms. It seems possible that it is another vector or symptom of the broader DoS activity being investigated here, although a separate DoS or a bug cannot yet be ruled out.

passages:
A relay operator reports a sustained circuit-building DoS against their guard relay family, starting 2026-06-25 23:00 UTC and still ongoing as of 2026-07-10. 

Source: [tor-relays thread, "Abnormal Firewall-States since...", 10 Jul 2026.](https://lists.torproject.org/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/tor-relays@lists.torproject.org/thread/VCUWQJ7KECAOL5ADPFWGX5OMYPQJAWG3/)

## Observations as reported by the operator

Key signature: millions of near-idle circuits. Circuit and stream counts explode while bandwidth barely moves.

Reported deltas (Jun 25 - Jul 10 vs prior 15 days, fleet-wide via MetricsPort)

MetricChangeOpen circuits +719% (8x sustained, 20x at peak)

Onionskins processed+ 639% (7x)

Stream creation +1126% (12x)

Bandwidth +20%

All locations and providers (EU + NA) hit simultaneously with the same onset time.

Load arrives over existing OR connections: established TCP counts stayed flat.

There is an onion-service introduction component.

Pattern suggests network-wide or family-targeted, not host-specific.

Impact contained for their relays: DoS defenses engaged, zero TCP port exhaustion, zero global rate-limit events.

EU relays shed 10-20% of real traffic (closer to capacity). NA relays absorbed the load without shedding.

The symptom class matches previous DDoS attacks: 
- circuit creation floods overloading non-exit relays' 
- onionskin processing, plus an onion-service introduction component.

### Timeline (UTC)

Jun 22, 12:00-24:00: 12h precursor burst, open circuits ~8x normal, then two quiet days.

Jun 25, 23:00: onset. Onionskin processing ~2.5x within 30 minutes, open circuits ~6x within 3 hours.

Jun 26-27: first major waves. introduce2_rejected bursts an order of magnitude above normal (peak Jun 27 03:00). conn_rejected ~5x baseline, bursts to

~10x.

Jun 26-28: overload symptoms. Brief onionskin drops on a small subset of relays, OOM handler ~10x more active, Stable/Fast/Running flag counts dip ~5% (Guard -3%).

Jul 5, 08:00: peak, open circuits ~20x baseline.

Jul 6-10: slow decay, still ~5-6x baseline on Jul 10.
