passages:
This is https://hackerone.com/reports/3931869

## Executive Summary

Alice, a Tor client operator, enables v3 onion-service client authorization and stores an x25519 private key in an owner-only `ClientOnionAuthDir`. If that file loses one Base32 character, Tor rejects the malformed credential but writes the remaining 51 key characters to a WARN log even when `SafeLogging` is set to its default value of `1`. Eve, a separate log reader who cannot read Alice's client-auth directory, can therefore obtain a near-complete private key from Tor's logs. This is not remotely triggerable, it does not expose a well-formed key, and the test did not connect to or decrypt an onion service.

| Field | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Asset | Tor core, v3 onion-service client authorization |
| Assessed release | Tor 0.4.9.11 |
| Earliest verified affected release | Tor 0.3.5.1-alpha |
| Fixed release | None identified; the statement is also present on the public `main` branch inspected on 2026-08-11 |
| Weakness | CWE-532, Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File |
| Suggested severity | Low |

I reviewed the exact Tor 0.4.9.11 source, traced the relevant logging statement to its introducing change, checked the first feature release and current public branch, and reran the supplied PoC against the exact locally built binary. The run used a container with networking disabled, `DisableNetwork 1`, an owner-only auth directory, `SafeLogging 1`, and a dummy key. The malformed 51-character key appeared verbatim at WARN; a well-formed 52-character control key did not appear in the log.

The suggested Low severity reflects a real disclosure of secret key material with substantial prerequisites. An operator must enable the optional client-auth feature, a key file must be malformed in a spec

ific way, and a second principal must be able to read Tor's logs while being unable to read the auth directory. No cross-principal log access or successful descriptor decryption was demonstrated in the lab.

## Background

`ClientOnionAuthDir` is an opt-in Tor configuration setting. Each `.auth_private` file has four colon-separated fields:

```text
:descriptor:x25519:
```

In Tor 0.4.9.11, `hs_client_service_authorization_t.enc_seckey` is a Curve25519 secret key used to compute the decryption keys that let an authorized client decrypt an onion-service descriptor (`src/feature/hs/hs_client.h`, `hs_client_service_authorization_t`). Tor checks that `ClientOnionAuthDir` is private before enumerating it. On Unix-like systems, the directory helper creates private directories with mode `0700` and rejects inappropriate permissions unless a specifically permitted group mode applies (`src/lib/fs/dir.c`, `check_private_dir`).

Tor also documents `SafeLogging 1` as replacing all potentially sensitive strings, with an exception for messages more verbose than Notice. WARN is less verbose than Notice, so the documented exception does not apply here. `SafeLogging` defaults to `1` in `src/app/config/config.c`.

The relevant boundary is not between a remote user and Tor. It is between the principal that can read the client-auth directory and a lower-trust principal or system that can read logs. Tor supports stderr, stdout, syslog, file, controller, and API-backed logging. Tor-created file logs are opened with mode `0640`, but actual log readers, groups, collectors, support bundles, and retention rules are deployment-specific. The PoC captured stderr and did not establish that a particular production deployment exposes logs to another principal.

## Vulnerability Details

### Source-to-s

r branch, not this decoder-error branch. The second branch is included because it logs the same private-key field at the same severity for the same reason, but its practical recoverability depends on how the full-length input is malformed and was not measured here.

The parser later wipes `seckey_b32` before freeing it:

```c
if (seckey_b32) {
 memwipe(seckey_b32, 0, strlen(seckey_b32));
}
```

That cleanup protects the parser's in-memory copy after use, but it cannot remove the copy already emitted to a log destination.

### Release history

The length check and raw WARN interpolation were introduced by commit `3695ef63` on 2018-09-07. The change was titled `HSv3: Don't assert when reading bad client-side privkeys.` Its purpose was defensive input handling, but the new error path printed the rejected private-key field.

Tor 0.3.5.1-alpha is the earliest released snapshot I verified with the logging statement. Its ChangeLog identifies it as the first 0.3.5.x release and the release that added client authorization for v3 onion services. The earlier `tor-0.3.5.0-alpha-dev` snapshot did not contain this parser. I also verified the vulnerable statement in the assessed Tor 0.4.9.11 release and in the public `main` branch at commit `3bfb4986`, dated 2026-08-06. I did not inspect every intermediate patch tag individually, so I am not claiming that each intermediate release was separately confirmed. I found no public fixing change or fixed release for this exact sink.

### Public duplicate review

A read-only search of the public Tor issue tracker for client-auth private-key logging, `SafeLogging`, `.auth_private`, and the exact Base32 error wording did not locate an issue describing this source-to-sink path. Private HackerOne reports are not visible, so final duplicate status

remains unknown.

The closest public issue I found is [Tor issue 29135](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/29135), which reported that a failed client-auth connection logged an entire received onion-service descriptor at WARN. That issue concerns a different input, function, and sink. [Tor issue 29040](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/29040) concerns a crash caused by duplicate local credentials, and [Tor issue 27896](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/27896) concerns Base32 padding acceptance. Neither describes disclosure of the local client-auth private-key field.

## Exploitability Analysis

The demonstrated primitive is narrow but concrete: a 51-character prefix of a 52-character Base32-encoded x25519 private key is copied from an owner-only credential file into a WARN log while safe logging is enabled.

For the exact truncation used in the PoC, enumerating all 32 possible final Base32 characters produces exactly two distinct 32-byte private keys. The original dummy key is one of those two values. The reduction from 32 suffix characters to two binary keys follows from the unused padding bits in the last Base32 character of a 32-byte value.

This does not establish universal key recovery. To turn the two candidates into a usable key, Eve would also need a way to associate the log line with the correct onion address and a reliable oracle. If Eve knows the onion address and can obtain the corresponding encrypted descriptor, attempting descriptor decryption with both candidates may distinguish the correct key. That chain was not executed, and no access to an onion service was demonstrated.

The complete practical prerequisites are:

1. Alice enables the optional `ClientOnionAuthDir` feature.
2. A correctly

structured `.auth_private` file contains a private key truncated to 51 Base32 characters. This can arise from operator or deployment-tool error; no remote trigger was identified.
3. Tor starts or otherwise reads that credential file with WARN messages directed to a log destination.
4. Eve can read that log destination or a copied support bundle, but cannot already read `ClientOnionAuthDir`.
5. For the conditional stronger impact, Eve can associate the logged prefix with an onion address and obtain a descriptor or another reliable check for the two candidate keys.

The positive runtime test fixed `SafeLogging` to `1`, used directory mode `0700` and file mode `0600`, supplied a 51-character dummy key, and observed the complete 51-character value in stderr at WARN. The negative control used the corresponding well-formed 52-character key under otherwise identical conditions and confirmed that it did not appear in stderr. Both Tor processes exited cleanly. Networking was disabled at both the container and Tor layers, which rules out a public service response as the source of the observed line.

Important limitations and counterevidence are:

- A well-formed key is not logged by this path.
- The malformed file is rejected, so Alice cannot use that file successfully until it is corrected.
- The trigger is local configuration state, not remote network input.
- If logs and the auth directory are readable only by the same principal, this finding creates no new principal boundary.
- The PoC did not verify syslog, a file log, a controller subscriber, a support workflow, descriptor decryption, or onion-service access.
- Deployment prevalence for `ClientOnionAuthDir` and cross-principal log access is unknown.

These constraints are why Low is more appropriate than Medium despite the

sensitivity of the field.

## Proof of Concept

The sibling `poc/poc.py` script is a bounded local reproducer. It creates temporary `0700` data and auth directories, writes only the included dummy fixture at mode `0600`, runs Tor with `DisableNetwork 1`, disables SocksPort and ORPort, captures stderr, terminates the exact process after startup, and removes the temporary directories. It runs both the malformed input and the well-formed negative control.

The preserved test used an exact Tor 0.4.9.11 binary with SHA-256:

```text
534c61c8f701a3052bb2be0986707a4234c341577cc1ad75abfa3dbb51a246ba
```

To reproduce safely, build the official `tor-0.4.9.11` tag in a disposable local environment, ensure that binary is selected as `tor`, block outbound networking at the container or VM layer, and run from this report directory:

```sh
cd poc
TOR_BINARY=tor POC_OUTPUT=result.json python3 poc.py
```

`TOR_BINARY` can instead name a report-relative executable. The script prints and optionally writes a JSON record containing the tested binary hash, permissions, configuration, matching log line, candidate count, negative-control result, and process exit codes.

The preserved run produced:

```json
{
 "auth_directory_mode": "0o700",
 "auth_file_mode": "0o600",
 "disable_network": true,
 "distinct_32_byte_keys_consistent_with_logged_prefix": 2,
 "input_key_length": 51,
 "matching_log_lines": [
 "Aug 11 05:40:58.000 [warn] Client authorization encoded base32 private key length is invalid: rcow3dfavmyanyqvhwnvnmfdqw34ydtrgv7jnelmqs4wi4uuxrc"
 ],
 "original_key_is_in_reconstructed_set": true,
 "safe_logging": 1,
 "schema": "tor-hs-client-auth-key-log-poc-v2",
 "secret_appears_in_stderr": true,
 "target_revision": "f3d28b2e0978ca075ec324834bec077673478ded",
 "tor_exit_code": 0,
 "tor_sha2

56": "534c61c8f701a3052bb2be0986707a4234c341577cc1ad75abfa3dbb51a246ba",
 "vulnerable": true,
 "well_formed_control_passed": tru

e,
 "well_formed_control_tor_exit_code": 0,
 "well_formed_key_appears_in_stderr": false
}
```

The logged value is the dummy fixture embedded in the PoC, not a production credential. The executed container used `--network none` and automatic removal; no test container remained after the run. The script removes its temporary credential and data directories. The intentionally preserved `result.json` remains beside the script for reviewer verification.

## Remediation

Private-key material should never be included in log messages, even when an operator disables `SafeLogging`. The most robust fix is to remove `seckey_b32` from both malformed-key warnings:

```c
if (strlen(seckey_b32) != BASE32_NOPAD_LEN(CURVE25519_SECKEY_LEN)) {
 log_warn(LD_REND, "Client authorization encoded base32 private key "
 "length is invalid");
 goto err;
}
```

Apply the same treatment to the Base32 decode failure. If diagnostic context is required, log only a safely handled filename or an error category, never the credential value. Passing the key through a SafeLogging helper would protect the default mode, but unconditional omission is preferable because `SafeLogging 0` should not turn private-key material into routine diagnostic output.

The existing `memwipe()` should remain. It is useful defense in depth for memory lifetime, although it cannot undo an earlier log write.

Add regression coverage to `src/test/test_hs_client.c` around `test_parse_auth_file_content()`:

1. Capture WARN output while parsing a 51-character key with `SafeLogging 1`; assert that the secret is absent.
2. Repeat with a full-length string containing an invalid Base32 character; assert that the supplied field is absent.
3. Repeat with `SafeLogging 0`; assert that private-key material is still absent.
4. Confirm that both

malformed values are rejected and still produce an actionable generic error.
5. Confirm that a valid 52-character key parses successfully without a WARN containing the key.

## Summary

Tor 0.4.9.11 copies a malformed v3 onion client-auth private-key field into WARN logs without applying SafeLogging redaction. The exact offline run showed that a one-character-truncated key is logged verbatim despite `SafeLogging 1`, reducing the dummy 32-byte key to exactly two candidates, while the valid-key control was not logged. The first verified affected release is 0.3.5.1-alpha, and the public `main` branch inspected on 2026-08-11 still contains the statement; no fixed release was identified.

The security consequence depends on a real separation between credential-file access and log access. No remote trigger, production log reader, descriptor decryption, or onion-service access was demonstrated, so the report is intentionally scoped as Low severity.

OpenAI Codex Security assisted with source review and report drafting. I manually verified the source-to-impact chain, scope, duplicate status, severity, and reproduced the behavior locally using the attached bounded, network-disabled PoC. No public Tor infrastructure or user data was accessed.

## Impact

A log reader who cannot access the owner-only ClientOnionAuthDir can receive 51 of 52 Base32 characters of a malformed x25519 client-auth private key from WARN output even with SafeLogging=1. The reproduced prefix reduced the 32-byte dummy key to exactly two candidates, which can materially undermine onion-service client authorization where log access is less trusted than credential-file access. The issue is local and configuration-dependent; no remote trigger, production key, or onion-service decryption was demonstrated.

sources.title: [tor-announce] [RELEASE] New C-tor 0.4.9.15
passages:
Greetings,

We just released tor 0.4.9.15. Here is the announcement:
https://forum.torproject.org/t/security-release-0-4-9-15/22332

For more information on the new DoS defenses, see:
https://lists.torproject.org/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/tor-relays＠lists.torproject.org/thread/DO63TMBKGPNCUG2UBNBZ6PSJOXMP4VM4/

Here is the ChangeLog:

Changes in version 0.4.9.15 - 2026-10-28
 This is another security release that includes new DoS defenses against large
 volumes of directory requests received by relays. Another significant change
 is that the HSDir flag is now sticky, meaning it persists across restarts.
 This release primarily affects relays so please upgrade as soon as possible.

 o Directory authority changes:
 - Directory authorities now list the protocol capabilities
 "RELAY_NEGOTIATE_SUBPROTO" and "RELAY_CRYPT_CGO" as required for
 relays. This change will allow clients to assume that all relays
 support Counter Galois Onion encryption, and use it even for
 relays not currently listed in the consensus.
 - Directory authorities now list the protocol capabilities
 "DESC_NO_TAP" and "MICRODESC_NO_TAP" as required for clients and
 relays. This changes will allow us to remove TAP keys from onion
 desciptors and microdescriptors, saving a great deal of directory
 bandwidth. Because of this change, Tor versions 0.4.8 and earlier
 will no longer work on the network.

 o Major features (directory authority):
 - Directory authorities provide a new consensus method that omits
 _all_ TAP keys and family lists from microdescriptors. This change
 is not compatible with 0.4.8, but 0.4.8 is no longer supported. It
 will save a great deal of directory bandwidth.

 o Major bugfixes (directory authority):
 - Correctly handle the middle-only flag at directory authorities, to
 prevent i

t from getting clobbered by a newly created consensus.
 This prevents flip-flopping of the middleonly flag. Fixes bug
 41457; bugfix on 0.4.9.14.

 o Minor features (denial of service mitigation):
 - Directory caches can now rate limit BEGIN_DIR cells per circuit,
 independently of the exit stream creation limit. This is
 controlled by the new DoSBeginDirRateEnabled, DoSBeginDirRate,
 DoSBeginDirBurst and DoSBeginDirDefenseType consensus parameters
 and torrc options, enabled by default. Refusals are reported in
 the heartbeat and in the
 relay_dos_total{type="begindir_rate_rejected"} metric. Part of
 ticket 41411.
 - Directory caches can now refuse any BEGIN_DIR after the first one
 on a circuit from an authenticated relay. This is controlled by
 the new DoSBeginDirLimitEnabled consensus parameter, disabled by
 default. Refusals are reported in the heartbeat and in the
 relay_dos_total{type="begindir_rejected"} metric. Closes
 ticket 41411.
 - Onion service directories now accept at most one descriptor fetch
 or upload per circuit from an authenticated relay, and close the
 circuit on any later one. This holds even when the BEGIN_DIR per-
 circuit limit is disabled.

 o Minor features (directory authority):
 - Directory authorities now assign the HSDir flag to a relay that
 had it in a recent consensus even if its uptime is below
 MinUptimeHidServDirectoryV2, so a restart no longer costs a relay
 its HSDir flag for 96 hours. All other HSDir requirements still
 apply. Fixes ticket 41175.

 o Minor features (directory performance):
 - Filter malformed directory request digests in linear time,
 avoiding repeated list shifting when rejecting invalid entries.
 Preserve digest ordering and the existing sorting and
 deduplication behavior.
 - Summarize invalid directory reque

st digests and consensus diff
 header digests once per parsing call, instead of logging each
 rejected entry. Omit rejected digest strings from these
 diagnostics and from invalid consensus diff URL diagnostics.

 o Minor features (fallbackdir):
 - Regenerate fallback directories generated on October 28, 2026.

 o Minor features (geoip data):
 - Update the geoip files to match the IPFire Location Database, as
 retrieved on 2026/10/28.

 o Minor features (performance):
 - Track connection membership in the active linked and closeable
 lists using indices, and update those indices when removing
 entries. Use the connection array index for membership checks and
 clear it on removal. This avoids repeated global list scans during
 activation and teardown. Report inconsistent indices nonfatally
 and recover with a list search before modifying the list.

 o Minor features (relay):
 - Relays now use a separate circuit for each directory request, so
 that directory caches can later limit relays to one BEGIN_DIR
 per circuit.

 o Minor bugfixes (conflux, control port):
 - Refuse ATTACHSTREAM onto a conflux circuit that has not finished
 linking. Such a leg is open but a stream that you attach to it
 will be silently dropped from the circuit (with a BUG() warning)
 when the set linked. Fixes bug 41454; bugfix on 0.4.8.1-alpha.

 o Minor bugfixes (onion service, control port):
 - Fix a memory leak of the parsed signing-key certificate and
 superencrypted blob (roughly the size of the descriptor) on every
 HSPOST control-port command. Fixes bug 41455; bugfix
 on 0.3.3.1-alpha.

 o Minor bugfixes (scheduling):
 - Fix a bug in smartlist_pqueue_remove that could schedulers (for
 circuits within a channel, and for channels on the internet
 connection) to serve items in the wrong order,

leading to
 temporary starvation for higher-priority circuits. Fixes bug
 41428; bugfix on 0.2.2.7-alpha.

-- 
MCgfKt8Z71zgn/ZfkxQViFHsfNFGHjprU2EQX+0o9HQ=

passages.text: labeling as security embargo, because @ahf says that's how he will notice it

passages.author: arma
passages.text:
There is also a broader class of attack here, where there could be all sorts of strings that we write into controller events / responses without proper sanitization.

This is a fun one because there is a path where some external entity gives it to us, but it's a pretty esoteric path. Are there more like that? Probably, and maybe some that we get from the network i.e. that are more risky.

The proper response here would be to go through the controller lines and audit which entries are intended to be non-quoted-strings, and wrap them with ```escaped()``` by default.

passages.author: arma
passages.text: In terms of "bugfix on", I picked the Tor version where we unveiled the v1 controller protocol. I think maybe the v0 controller protocol was robust to this type of attack.

passages.author: arma
passages.text:
https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/merge_requests/1025 has the basic fix.

I targeted git main (Tor 0.5.0) because I don't think this is enough of a security issue for us to put it into the current stable.

I recommend un-confidentialing this ticket as soon as is practical -- it is fine for it to go public even though we won't have an 0.5.0 release for a good while.

In terms of hacker one bounty, based on https://hackerone.com/torproject I would put this one somewhere between "tshirt" and "low" depending on how generous the decider is feeling at the time -- it requires a torrc option that nobody sets, and then also a local attacker, and then also a controller program that you can trick into some other potential misbehavior.

passages.author: arma
passages.text:
For those debugging: commit bf6702cf8b (Tor 0.1.2.5-alpha) is when the AllowNonRFC953Hostnames feature went in. It's been off (i.e. in the 'safe' setting) for all of its life.

So I would triage this one as "you can create a bit of mischief if the user has somehow set this esoteric setting that they are unlikely to set."

Worth fixing but I agree with Nick, minor.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text:
Sounds real though I haven't verified it.

Seems relatively minor, though, since:
 - The user needs to set a pretty unused option.
 - The user needs to be running an application that is willing to make connections to places with hostnames containing CRLF, and that the attacker can cause to do so. (I think most web browsers just won't do this, right?)
 - The user needs to be running a controller that will act in such as way as to harm user security if it sees an attacker-crafted event.

passages:
PoC: Tor control-event CRLF injection via SOCKS hostname (stream-status path)

Reported via [HackerOne](https://hackerone.com/reports/3751660)

---

**Vulnerability:** CRLF injection into control STREAM status events via SOCKS hostname 
**Weakness:** CWE-93, Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences 
**Affected asset:** C Tor daemon (`tor`) 
**Severity:** Low (CVSS 3.1 `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N = 3.7`) 
**Tested commit:** `2d8fb125e4fd7148570aabd12aa29a45a5a6e902`

## Summary

When `AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1` is configured, Tor's SOCKS5 server accepts hostnames
containing arbitrary bytes, including `\r` and `\n`. The hostname is stored verbatim in
`socks_request->address` via `strlcpy()` in `proto_socks.c`. When Tor later emits a STREAM
status event for that connection, `write_stream_target_to_buf()` copies the attacker-controlled
address into the event buffer with a raw `%s`, and `send_control_event()` writes it to every
connected controller without CRLF sanitization.

The result is control-event injection: an unauthenticated SOCKS client can insert fake event
lines such as `650 CIRC 1 BUILT` into the control-protocol stream seen by concurrent controllers.
Any controller that parses events line by line may misinterpret the injected line as a legitimate
Tor event.

## One-command repro

```bash
# From the case root directory:
bash poc/stream-status/build.sh
bash poc/stream-status/run.sh
```

Expected: line containing `INJECTION_CONFIRMED` in stdout, exit 0.

## Manual reproduction steps

1. Start Tor with `ControlPort=9051`, `SocksPort=9050`, `AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1`, and a
 known control password or cookie-auth setup.
1. Connect a controller to `127.0.0.1:9051`, authenticate, and subscribe to STREAM events with:

 ```text
 SETEVENTS STREAM
 ```

1. From a

separate SOCKS5 client, send a raw CONNECT request to `127.0.0.1:9050` using a
 length-prefixed domainname containing embedded CR/LF bytes, for example:

 ```text
 x\r\n650 CIRC 1 BUILT\r\n.example.com
 ```

1. Capture raw bytes on the controller connection.
1. Observe that one STREAM event is split into multiple apparent event lines, including a fake
 injected `650 CIRC 1 BUILT` line.

## What to look for

```
[PASS] INJECTION_CONFIRMED: STREAM NEW event contains injected CRLF bytes; fake event line: '650 CIRC 1 BUILT'
```

The raw event bytes on the controller socket contain `\r\n650 CIRC` — a
fake event line inserted between the legitimate STREAM event's first and
second parts. A naive line-oriented controller parser treats it as a real
CIRC event.

## Network

The container runs with `--network=none`. No external connections are made.
Tor starts in loopback-only mode inside the container.

## Severity

Low (HackerOne rubric). Requires `AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1` (operator
opt-in, non-default). Unauthenticated SOCKS client, no control-port
credential needed. Impact: event-stream desynchronization for concurrent
controllers.

## Relevant source paths

- `src/feature/control/control_fmt.c:42` (`write_stream_target_to_buf()` raw address copy)
- `src/feature/control/control_events.c:808` (calls `write_stream_target_to_buf()`)
- `src/feature/control/control_events.c:906-912` (`send_control_event()` emits `%s` buffer)
- `src/app/transport/proto_socks.c:197` (`strlcpy()` preserves hostname bytes verbatim)
- `src/feature/nodelist/addressmap.c:1085-1086` (`AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1` bypass gate)

## Impact

This issue allows an unauthenticated SOCKS client to inject fake event lines into the Tor control
event stream received by concurrent controllers. The impact is limited b

ecause exploitation
requires `AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1`, which is a non-default operator opt-in, but no control-port
credentials are needed once that prerequisite is enabled.

Controllers or automation that parse each CRLF-terminated `650` line as a separate trusted event
may become desynchronized and act on forged state transitions.

passages:
-----BEGIN PGP SIGNED MESSAGE-----
Hash: SHA512

Hello.

Apparently, the attacker has returned and successfully stripped the
HSDir flag from two of my relays in a few hours. One attack saw high
asymmetric egress and one saw high asymmetric ingress (although not
nearly as much as the old attacks, so total bandwidth stayed about the
same). Both relays lost their HSDir flags as a result.

The high-ingress attack (100 Mbps in, 15 Mbps out) did not cause any
noticeable CPU increase but caused my entire swap partition to fill up
and caused severe thrashing. The high-egress attack (30 Mbps in, 130
Mbps out) only increased memory usage slightly but pegged the CPU at
100% the entire time.

As with the last attack, the MetricsPort and ControlPort become fully
unresponsive, preventing me from easily collecting diagnostics. I did
manage to get some metrics from the victim of the egress attack. Some

`maatuska`'s was suffering from a 2.5h power outage on 2025-10-27 and is since then reporting way fewer relays having the Guard flags in its vote than the consensus, according to mails sent by DocTor to the consensus-health mailing list.

One theory was that the power outage might have tricked `maatuska` into that behavior (Stable and HSDir flags are affected as well) and that the situation would over time resolve itself.

With the [first report](https://lists.torproject.org/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/tor-consensus-health@lists.torproject.org/thread/RX2LZ3RR37IEJGJ3U5Y4R2K7FS24EMG5/) hitting the list we got:
```
NOTICE: maatuska had 2552 Guard flags in its vote but the consensus had 5859
```
but after almost 4 days the number has not been rising substantially let alone from resolving that problem. The [latest report](https://lists.torproject.org/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/tor-consensus-health@lists.torproject.org/thread/WSN3U4MTB3QVOKTAUOUOPQ7A2452Y3R7/) says:

```

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: Calling this ~"Severity::low" because you need to control multiple authorities to exploit it.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: Looks real. Also looks like an easy fix.

passages:
We got this one on security@

## Summary

dirvote.c:2329 uses %d to format uint32_t bandwidth_kb during
consensus generation. Three colluding directory authorities can wedge
consensus on ALL honest authorities — a network-wide DoS.

## Attack Chain (PoC-confirmed)

1. 3 malicious authorities run a real reachable relay X, publish its
descriptor to 2 honest authorities
2. Vote X as Running with Bandwidth=4294967295
3. All honest authorities compute median over 5 listing votes = huge value
4. %d renders "w Bandwidth=-1"
5. Self-check re-parse fails → networkstatus_compute_consensus() returns NULL
6. No consensus published network-wide, repeatable hourly

Normally 3-of-9 malicious authorities cannot stop consensus (6 honest
sigs ≥ 5) — this bug amplifies them across a real security boundary.

## Fix

One character: %d → %u.

## PoC

Compiled against real tor_parse_ulong + median_uint32; confirms all 4
chain steps. Available on request.

## Dedup

No prior CVE or public issue found for this specific bug.

sources.title: New Release: Tor Browser 16.0
passages:
Tor Browser 16.0 is now available for Desktop and Android. This is our first stable release based on Firefox ESR 153, incorporating a year's worth of changes that have been shipped upstream in Firefox. As part of this process, we've also completed our annual ESR transition audit, where we reviewed and addressed over 270 Bugzilla issues covering changes in Firefox that could negatively affect the privacy and security of Tor Browser users.

The ongoing development of Tor Browser is made possible thanks to the support of our community. Every donation helps power the tools that let people browse freely and privately. Consider joining thousands of others who have already made a small contribution towards building a better internet for everyone.

What's new for Desktop?

Redesigned Settings

Tor Browser connects millions of people to the Tor network (and by extension, the free and open internet) out of the box. However, for those who need to circumvent advanced censorship, boost their security level, or tailor their browsing experience, clear and easy-to-use Settings are essential. To that end, Tor Browser 16.0 introduces a complete redesign of the Settings experience based on a parallel redesign shipped in Firefox in June. Improvements include a cleaner layout, updated navigation, and clearer labels and descriptions aimed at making settings easier to find, understand, and manage. Other noteworthy changes include:

The long-standing "General" page has been retired, with its contents distributed across new pages for Appearance, Downloads, Tabs and browsing, Accessibility and Languages.

Pages and components that are unique to Tor browser like Connection and Security Level have been rebuilt from scratch using Firefox's new components so they look and feel consistent with the re

st of Settings.

Some settings that, if enabled, could compromise your privacy or make your browser easier to fingerprint have either been hidden or feature clear warnings.

Fear not: your existing preferences will remain saved even if the original setting has moved or changed, and you can use the search bar at the top of Settings to find anything you're struggling to track down.

Generic window titles

Another new addition to Settings is the option to use generic window titles, which can be found under Privacy and security → Protections from third-party applications. Like most browsers, Tor Browser uses the title of the page you're currently viewing for the names of its windows. However, other applications on your computer or your operating system itself can read these titles without special permissions. When enabled, this option simply replaces all window titles with "Tor Browser" — preventing other software from snooping on your browsing history. As always, for more comprehensive protection from third-party applications on your device, we recommend using Tails.

For now, this option is strictly opt-in, as we did not have sufficient time during this release cycle to properly evaluate potential side-effects for users. In particular, we worry that enabling this setting may reduce the browser's usability for those who rely on accessibility tools (e.g. screen-readers) or those with highly customized systems (e.g. less-popular desktop managers, application switchers, etc). If you are one of these users, we would ask that you try using this setting, and report back any bugs or usability issues you find!

📣 Generic window titles have also been upstreamed to Firefox as part of the Tor Uplift Project. Advanced Firefox users can enable this feature by opening about:config and s

etting privacy.exposeContentTitleInWindow (for normal windows) and privacy.exposeContentTitleInWindow.pbm (for private browsing windows) to false.

New user manual

The Tor Browser manual, which can be found by visiting about:manual or through the application menu (☰) → Help → Tor Browser manual, has also received a complete revamp. Since the release of our new Support portal in 2025, the team has had to maintain two sets of documentation: one for the traditional manual that's available to read in Tor Browser, and another for the new Support site. With this release, we've solved that problem by replacing the older material in the Tor Browser manual with our latest and greatest help content from the new Support site. Like the previous iteration of the manual, the new version is bundled with Tor Browser for Desktop so it can be read offline, which comes in particularly handy when troubleshooting issues that prevent you from connecting to the Tor network.

Linux on ARM

Finally, after a year of testing, Tor Browser 16.0 now features native support for Linux computers with 64-bit ARM (AArch64) processors, such as Raspberry Pis and Apple Silicon Macs running Linux. If you have been relying on Tor Browser Alpha for support for these devices, we recommend switching over to the stable release channel unless you plan to continue testing Alpha releases. Meanwhile, Tor Browser 16.0 follows Firefox in ending support for 32-bit x86 Linux computers. Fortunately, very few people should be affected, as we currently receive around 200 update checks from this platform a day, down from a peak of around 4,000 in 2019. Most remaining 32-bit users should be able to switch to the 64-bit version unless they're running outdated hardware or versions of Linux.

What's new for Android?

Tor Browse

r for Android has also benefited from Mozilla's ongoing work to modernize Firefox, as seen in the Settings redesign on desktop. Over the past year, Firefox has been gradually transitioning to Jetpack Compose — Google's newest framework for building native Android interfaces. In this release, we've made significant progress applying the same changes to Tor Browser. As a result, large swaths of Tor Browser's user interface has been updated to Material Design 3 — the latest iteration of Google's design language for Android — with more yet to come in future releases.

Google Play limits the size of apps distributed as APKs to 100 MB. Since Firefox for Android continues to grow with each release, keeping Tor Browser within this limit has been an ongoing challenge — for example, this issue has prevented us from bundling Tor Browser's manual on Android so that it can be accessed offline. Nevertheless, we've found various ways to reduce the size of our Android package over the years and stay within the limit. Most recently, this involved carefully and creatively compressing some of the built-in resources Firefox uses to display its interface.

What's in the works?

Tor Browser users can expect additional improvements over the next few months as we continue to refine the new Settings experience for desktop and Material Design 3 for Android. If you find a bug or have a suggestion for how we could improve this release, we'd love to hear your feedback.

The team is also working hard on a new and improved circuit display, coming soon to Tor Browser Alpha, which integrates site information directly into the circuit panel and can visualize more complex multi-path circuits. Multi-path circuits use additional relays to split your traffic into two paths that converge on a single exit, im

proving both connection speed and reliability. These circuits already exist for regular websites (but not onion sites) and are randomly assigned based on network availability. Although Tor Browser's traditional circuit display can only show a single path at a time, you have likely benefited from a multi-path circuit without even knowing it. What's more, this exciting update will mark the debut of the circuit display on Tor Browser for Android, which has been exclusive to desktop until now.

Contributions <3

Thanks to all of the teams across Tor, and the wider community, who contributed to this release. In particular, we'd like to extend our gratitude to the following volunteers who have contributed their expertise, labor, and time:

NoisyCoil

Soni

If you would like to contribute to a future release, please see our guide for new contributors to get started.

sources.title: Arti 2.8.0 released
passages:
Arti is our ongoing project to create a next-generation Tor implementation in Rust.
We're happy to announce the latest release, Arti 2.8.0.

This release continues our ongoing development towards using
Arti as a relay and as a directory authority,
with much of the work focusing on
computing the consensus from votes,
bootstrapping router descriptors and microdescriptors,
as well as relay bandwidth rate-limiting,
descriptor encoding, and the relay DNS cache implementation.
Additionally, we have made a number of cleanups and
clarifications to the Tor specification.

This release contains security fixes for a number of low-severity security issues.
We encourage arti and arti-client users,
especially those running onion services,
to upgrade as soon as possible.

As usual, there also are many under-the-hood improvements
to our infrastructure, testing, and documentation,
along with multiple bug fixes and internal cleanups.

For full details on what we've done, including API changes, security fixes,
and for information about many more minor and less-visible changes,
please see the CHANGELOG.

For more information on using Arti, see our top-level README,
and the documentation for the arti binary.

Thanks to everybody who's contributed to this release, including
5225225, Gaith Hallak, and manthan-lab.

Also, our deep thanks to our sponsors for funding the development of Arti!

passages.author: ahf
passages.text: Gonna go through these soon

passages.author: arma
passages.text: [still in state security-embargo awaiting action from @ahf -- fine to open up any time on our side, but maybe needs hackerone action first.]

passages.author: arma
passages.text: labeling as security embargo, because @ahf says that's how he will notice it

passages.author: arma
passages.text:
There is also a broader class of attack here, where there could be all sorts of strings that we write into controller events / responses without proper sanitization.

This is a fun one because there is a path where some external entity gives it to us, but it's a pretty esoteric path. Are there more like that? Probably, and maybe some that we get from the network i.e. that are more risky.

The proper response here would be to go through the controller lines and audit which entries are intended to be non-quoted-strings, and wrap them with ```escaped()``` by default.

passages.author: arma
passages.text: In terms of "bugfix on", I picked the Tor version where we unveiled the v1 controller protocol. I think maybe the v0 controller protocol was robust to this type of attack.

passages.author: arma
passages.text:
https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/merge_requests/1025 has the basic fix.

I targeted git main (Tor 0.5.0) because I don't think this is enough of a security issue for us to put it into the current stable.

I recommend un-confidentialing this ticket as soon as is practical -- it is fine for it to go public even though we won't have an 0.5.0 release for a good while.

In terms of hacker one bounty, based on https://hackerone.com/torproject I would put this one somewhere between "tshirt" and "low" depending on how generous the decider is feeling at the time -- it requires a torrc option that nobody sets, and then also a local attacker, and then also a controller program that you can trick into some other potential misbehavior.

Sounds real though I haven't verified it.

Seems relatively minor, though, since:
 - The user needs to set a pretty unused option.
 - The user needs to be running an application that is willing to make connections to places with hostnames containing CRLF, and that the attacker can cause to do so. (I think most web browsers just won't do this, right?)
 - The user needs to be running a controller that will act in such as way as to harm user security if it sees an attacker-crafted event.

passages:
PoC: Tor control-event CRLF injection via SOCKS hostname (stream-status path)

Reported via [HackerOne](https://hackerone.com/reports/3751660)

---

**Vulnerability:** CRLF injection into control STREAM status events via SOCKS hostname 
**Weakness:** CWE-93, Improper Neutralization of CRLF Sequences 
**Affected asset:** C Tor daemon (`tor`) 
**Severity:** Low (CVSS 3.1 `AV:N/AC:H/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:N/I:L/A:N = 3.7`) 
**Tested commit:** `2d8fb125e4fd7148570aabd12aa29a45a5a6e902`

## Summary

When `AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1` is configured, Tor's SOCKS5 server accepts hostnames
containing arbitrary bytes, including `\r` and `\n`. The hostname is stored verbatim in
`socks_request->address` via `strlcpy()` in `proto_socks.c`. When Tor later emits a STREAM
status event for that connection, `write_stream_target_to_buf()` copies the attacker-controlled
address into the event buffer with a raw `%s`, and `send_control_event()` writes it to every
connected controller without CRLF sanitization.

The result is control-event injection: an unauthenticated SOCKS client can insert fake event
lines such as `650 CIRC 1 BUILT` into the control-protocol stream seen by concurrent controllers.
Any controller that parses events line by line may misinterpret the injected line as a legitimate
Tor event.

## One-command repro

```bash
# From the case root directory:
bash poc/stream-status/build.sh
bash poc/stream-status/run.sh
```

Expected: line containing `INJECTION_CONFIRMED` in stdout, exit 0.

## Manual reproduction steps

1. Start Tor with `ControlPort=9051`, `SocksPort=9050`, `AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1`, and a
 known control password or cookie-auth setup.
1. Connect a controller to `127.0.0.1:9051`, authenticate, and subscribe to STREAM events with:

 ```text
 SETEVENTS STREAM
 ```

1. From a

separate SOCKS5 client, send a raw CONNECT request to `127.0.0.1:9050` using a
 length-prefixed domainname containing embedded CR/LF bytes, for example:

 ```text
 x\r\n650 CIRC 1 BUILT\r\n.example.com
 ```

1. Capture raw bytes on the controller connection.
1. Observe that one STREAM event is split into multiple apparent event lines, including a fake
 injected `650 CIRC 1 BUILT` line.

## What to look for

```
[PASS] INJECTION_CONFIRMED: STREAM NEW event contains injected CRLF bytes; fake event line: '650 CIRC 1 BUILT'
```

The raw event bytes on the controller socket contain `\r\n650 CIRC` — a
fake event line inserted between the legitimate STREAM event's first and
second parts. A naive line-oriented controller parser treats it as a real
CIRC event.

## Network

The container runs with `--network=none`. No external connections are made.
Tor starts in loopback-only mode inside the container.

## Severity

Low (HackerOne rubric). Requires `AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1` (operator
opt-in, non-default). Unauthenticated SOCKS client, no control-port
credential needed. Impact: event-stream desynchronization for concurrent
controllers.

## Relevant source paths

- `src/feature/control/control_fmt.c:42` (`write_stream_target_to_buf()` raw address copy)
- `src/feature/control/control_events.c:808` (calls `write_stream_target_to_buf()`)
- `src/feature/control/control_events.c:906-912` (`send_control_event()` emits `%s` buffer)
- `src/app/transport/proto_socks.c:197` (`strlcpy()` preserves hostname bytes verbatim)
- `src/feature/nodelist/addressmap.c:1085-1086` (`AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1` bypass gate)

## Impact

This issue allows an unauthenticated SOCKS client to inject fake event lines into the Tor control
event stream received by concurrent controllers. The impact is limited b

ecause exploitation
requires `AllowNonRFC953Hostnames=1`, which is a non-default operator opt-in, but no control-port
credentials are needed once that prerequisite is enabled.

Controllers or automation that parse each CRLF-terminated `650` line as a separate trusted event
may become desynchronized and act on forged state transitions.

passages:
Our fix for #41360, #41365, and #41366 prevents remotely-induced Guard rotation cases.

However, we did not change the code in `circuit_build_failed()` that marks `is_bad_for_new_circs = 1` for the channel.

This means that an adversary can still use these triggers (and the other ones David found while working on https://gitlab.torproject.org/dgoulet/tor-private/-/merge_requests/33) to cause clients to create an additional TLS connection to their existing Guard. 

This effect can be observed by [netflow adversaries](https://spec.torproject.org/proposals/344-protocol-info-leaks.html#131-netflow-observation), potentially allowing them to confirm that a particular client was taking a particular action.

This is much much less severe than inducing Guard rotation, since the outcome is not immediate or definite. Existing circuits will continue to use the "bad for new circuits" TLS connection. New circuits might use the other guard before creating a new TLS connection.

Still, this is not a great property. If we can fix it simply, we should.. However it might not be simple to fix without some additional mechanism to ensure we actually *do* give up on channels that are dead due to transient network conditions.

We should at least have an LLM enumerate as many of these cases as possible for us, so we can weigh if any of them would be useful for an adversary (such as one that wants to make an onion service use a new TLS connection, or one that wants to make a client use a new TLS connection once it has been observed to be doing some specific activity).

Cc: @dgoulet

passages:
Greetings,

We just released tor 0.4.9.15. Here is the announcement:
https://forum.torproject.org/t/security-release-0-4-9-15/22332

For more information on the new DoS defenses, see:
https://lists.torproject.org/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/tor-relays＠lists.torproject.org/thread/DO63TMBKGPNCUG2UBNBZ6PSJOXMP4VM4/

Here is the ChangeLog:

Changes in version 0.4.9.15 - 2026-10-28
 This is another security release that includes new DoS defenses against large
 volumes of directory requests received by relays. Another significant change
 is that the HSDir flag is now sticky, meaning it persists across restarts.
 This release primarily affects relays so please upgrade as soon as possible.

 o Directory authority changes:
 - Directory authorities now list the protocol capabilities
 "RELAY_NEGOTIATE_SUBPROTO" and "RELAY_CRYPT_CGO" as required for
 relays. This change will allow clients to assume that all relays
 support Counter Galois Onion encryption, and use it even for
 relays not currently listed in the consensus.
 - Directory authorities now list the protocol capabilities
 "DESC_NO_TAP" and "MICRODESC_NO_TAP" as required for clients and
 relays. This changes will allow us to remove TAP keys from onion
 desciptors and microdescriptors, saving a great deal of directory
 bandwidth. Because of this change, Tor versions 0.4.8 and earlier
 will no longer work on the network.

 o Major features (directory authority):
 - Directory authorities provide a new consensus method that omits
 _all_ TAP keys and family lists from microdescriptors. This change
 is not compatible with 0.4.8, but 0.4.8 is no longer supported. It
 will save a great deal of directory bandwidth.

 o Major bugfixes (directory authority):
 - Correctly handle the middle-only flag at directory authorities, to
 prevent i

t from getting clobbered by a newly created consensus.
 This prevents flip-flopping of the middleonly flag. Fixes bug
 41457; bugfix on 0.4.9.14.

 o Minor features (denial of service mitigation):
 - Directory caches can now rate limit BEGIN_DIR cells per circuit,
 independently of the exit stream creation limit. This is
 controlled by the new DoSBeginDirRateEnabled, DoSBeginDirRate,
 DoSBeginDirBurst and DoSBeginDirDefenseType consensus parameters
 and torrc options, enabled by default. Refusals are reported in
 the heartbeat and in the
 relay_dos_total{type="begindir_rate_rejected"} metric. Part of
 ticket 41411.
 - Directory caches can now refuse any BEGIN_DIR after the first one
 on a circuit from an authenticated relay. This is controlled by
 the new DoSBeginDirLimitEnabled consensus parameter, disabled by
 default. Refusals are reported in the heartbeat and in the
 relay_dos_total{type="begindir_rejected"} metric. Closes
 ticket 41411.
 - Onion service directories now accept at most one descriptor fetch
 or upload per circuit from an authenticated relay, and close the
 circuit on any later one. This holds even when the BEGIN_DIR per-
 circuit limit is disabled.

 o Minor features (directory authority):
 - Directory authorities now assign the HSDir flag to a relay that
 had it in a recent consensus even if its uptime is below
 MinUptimeHidServDirectoryV2, so a restart no longer costs a relay
 its HSDir flag for 96 hours. All other HSDir requirements still
 apply. Fixes ticket 41175.

 o Minor features (directory performance):
 - Filter malformed directory request digests in linear time,
 avoiding repeated list shifting when rejecting invalid entries.
 Preserve digest ordering and the existing sorting and
 deduplication behavior.
 - Summarize invalid directory reque

st digests and consensus diff
 header digests once per parsing call, instead of logging each
 rejected entry. Omit rejected digest strings from these
 diagnostics and from invalid consensus diff URL diagnostics.

 o Minor features (fallbackdir):
 - Regenerate fallback directories generated on October 28, 2026.

 o Minor features (geoip data):
 - Update the geoip files to match the IPFire Location Database, as
 retrieved on 2026/10/28.

 o Minor features (performance):
 - Track connection membership in the active linked and closeable
 lists using indices, and update those indices when removing
 entries. Use the connection array index for membership checks and
 clear it on removal. This avoids repeated global list scans during
 activation and teardown. Report inconsistent indices nonfatally
 and recover with a list search before modifying the list.

 o Minor features (relay):
 - Relays now use a separate circuit for each directory request, so
 that directory caches can later limit relays to one BEGIN_DIR
 per circuit.

 o Minor bugfixes (conflux, control port):
 - Refuse ATTACHSTREAM onto a conflux circuit that has not finished
 linking. Such a leg is open but a stream that you attach to it
 will be silently dropped from the circuit (with a BUG() warning)
 when the set linked. Fixes bug 41454; bugfix on 0.4.8.1-alpha.

 o Minor bugfixes (onion service, control port):
 - Fix a memory leak of the parsed signing-key certificate and
 superencrypted blob (roughly the size of the descriptor) on every
 HSPOST control-port command. Fixes bug 41455; bugfix
 on 0.3.3.1-alpha.

 o Minor bugfixes (scheduling):
 - Fix a bug in smartlist_pqueue_remove that could schedulers (for
 circuits within a channel, and for channels on the internet
 connection) to serve items in the wrong order,

leading to
 temporary starvation for higher-priority circuits. Fixes bug
 41428; bugfix on 0.2.2.7-alpha.

-- 
MCgfKt8Z71zgn/ZfkxQViFHsfNFGHjprU2EQX+0o9HQ=

sources.title: Tor falls back to OpenSSL's default TLS groups when built against OpenSSL 4.x

passages.author: ahf
passages.text: Talked with Nick after the security meeting. Let's ignore the LibreSSL approach to this for now. Nick has an idea about making progress here 😎

passages.author: ahf
passages.text:
@nickm if we end up falling back to calling `SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list()` with just one group per iteration, then we can get the LibreSSL string in at the same time and solve: https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/41300

I didn't get any feedback from the LibreSSL people on extracting the used algorithm when I asked on their IRC channel sadly. They have different (and maybe missing?) API's for this compared to OpenSSL.

passages.author: ahf
passages.text: What is it that stops us from just using what the library wants to use? Right now LibreSSL also uses another string format that OpenSSL for this, and it seems to me like this is going to break again in the future?

passages.author: arma
passages.text:
A friend also reported this bug from their relay, running on "FreeBSD OpenSSL 3.6.5"

(same scary "[warn] No lists of TLS groups were supported. Using library defaults" line)

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: Looks like a must-fix to me :p

passages.author: ahf
passages.text: @nickm your thoughts on this? It seems like this selection logic keeps changing in OpenSSL :-/

passages:
tor 0.4.9.16 linked against OpenSSL 4.0.x or 4.1.0 logs at startup:

 [warn] No lists of TLS groups were supported. Using library defaults

and then runs with OpenSSL's default group list instead of the one chosen in
`src/lib/tls/tortls_openssl.c`. The same binary built against OpenSSL 3.5.9 logs

 [notice] Set list of supported TLS groups to: ?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:P-224

## Affected versions

tor 0.4.9.16, and `main` as of 2026-11-09, which has the same code, with any
OpenSSL 4.x built with the default configuration. OpenSSL 3.5 to 3.6 are not
affected.

## Root cause

`tor_tls_context_new()` tries three group lists in order with
`SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list()`. Every list contains `P-224` without the `?`
(ignore-if-unsupported) prefix:

 "?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:P-224" (OpenSSL >= 3.5.0)
 "P-256:X25519:P-224"
 "P-256:P-224"

OpenSSL 4.0.0 compiles the TLS groups RFC 8422 deprecates out by default.
CHANGES.md, "Changes between 3.6 and 4.0.0 [14 Apr 2026]"
(https://github.com/openssl/openssl/blob/openssl-4.0.0/CHANGES.md), says:

 Support of deprecated elliptic curves in TLS according to [RFC 8422] was
 disabled at compile-time by default. To enable it, use the
 `enable-tls-deprecated-ec` configuration option.

The change is https://github.com/openssl/openssl/pull/29658. INSTALL.md lists
the groups it covers: "the Koblitz curves, secp160r1, secp160r2, secp192r1,
secp224r1, and the binary Elliptic curves". In
`providers/common/capabilities.c`, the secp224r1 and P-224 entries are inside
`#ifndef OPENSSL_NO_TLS_DEPRECATED_EC`.

OpenSSL rejects a group list as a whole when it names an unknown group without
`?`. So all three lists fail, and tor falls back to the library defaults.
OpenSSL puts nothing on the error q

ueue, so tor has nothing more to log.

## Consequence

OpenSSL 4.1.0's default list is:

 ?*X25519MLKEM768:?SecP256r1MLKEM768:?curveSM2MLKEM768 / ?*X25519:?secp256r1 /
 ?X448:?secp384r1:?secp521r1 / ?curveSM2 / ?ffdhe2048:?ffdhe3072

Observed on tor processes running with it:

- **As a client**, tor sends X25519MLKEM768 and X25519 key shares instead of
 X25519MLKEM768 and P-256.
 - Against a peer that accepts only P-256, which is the case the source
 comment keeps `*P-256` for, the server answers with a HelloRetryRequest.
 The handshake costs an extra round trip.
 - Against a relay on OpenSSL 3.0 to 3.4 ("P-256:X25519"), X25519 is
 negotiated.
- **As a relay**, tor accepts groups the chosen list excludes. ffdhe2048,
 secp384r1 and x448 were each negotiated by a client offering only that group.
 With the chosen list, the same handshakes fail (alert 40).
- **Between two tor processes on OpenSSL 4.x**, X25519MLKEM768 is still
 negotiated.

## Reproduction

Build tor 0.4.9.16 against OpenSSL 4.1.0 (default `./Configure`) and start it
offline:

 tor --DisableNetwork 1 --SocksPort 0 --Log "notice stdout" --DataDirectory /tmp/td

Or call OpenSSL 4.1.0 directly:

 SSL_CTX *ctx = SSL_CTX_new(TLS_method());
 SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list(ctx, "P-256:P-224"); /* returns 0 */
 SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list(ctx, "P-256"); /* returns 1 */
 SSL_CTX_set1_groups_list(ctx, "P-256:?P-224"); /* returns 1 */

## Fix

Mark P-224 optional in the list used only with OpenSSL 3.5.0 and later. Every
OpenSSL that passes that gate understands `?`. The two older lists are only
reached below 3.5.0, where P-224 is always compiled in.

 --- a/src/lib/tls/tortls_openssl.c
 +++ b/src/lib/tls/tortls_openssl.c
 @@ -571,7 +571,7 @@
 // be the same. We can't prefer P-256 in one, and X25519 in another.
 {
 OPENSSL_V_SE

RIES(3,5,0),
 - "?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:P-224"
 + "?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:?P-224"
 },
 { 0, "P-256:X25519:P-224" },
 { 0, "P-256:P-224" },

The comment above the table may need updating too. "We do insist on the
presence of P-256 and P-224" no longer holds for P-224 on OpenSSL 4.x. There,
the group is unavailable unless OpenSSL is rebuilt with
`enable-tls-deprecated-ec`.

## Verification

tor 0.4.9.16 with the patch, against OpenSSL 4.1.0:

 [notice] Set list of supported TLS groups to: ?*X25519MLKEM768 / ?SecP256r1MLKEM768 / *P-256:?X25519:?P-224

There is no warning.

- **As a client**, it sends X25519MLKEM768 and P-256 key shares, and completes
 in one round trip against a P-256-only server.
- **As a relay**, it rejects ffdhe2048, P-384 and X448, and negotiates
 X25519MLKEM768 with a default client.

The patched build against OpenSSL 3.5.9 logs the same notice (with `?P-224`).
Its ClientHello offers the same set of groups as the unpatched 3.5.9 build,
and secp224r1 is still advertised.

passages:
A relay operator reports a sustained circuit-building DoS against their guard relay family, starting 2026-06-25 23:00 UTC and still ongoing as of 2026-07-10. 

Source: [tor-relays thread, "Abnormal Firewall-States since...", 10 Jul 2026.](https://lists.torproject.org/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/tor-relays@lists.torproject.org/thread/VCUWQJ7KECAOL5ADPFWGX5OMYPQJAWG3/)

## Observations as reported by the operator

Key signature: millions of near-idle circuits. Circuit and stream counts explode while bandwidth barely moves.

Reported deltas (Jun 25 - Jul 10 vs prior 15 days, fleet-wide via MetricsPort)

MetricChangeOpen circuits +719% (8x sustained, 20x at peak)

Onionskins processed+ 639% (7x)

Stream creation +1126% (12x)

Bandwidth +20%

All locations and providers (EU + NA) hit simultaneously with the same onset time.

Load arrives over existing OR connections: established TCP counts stayed flat.

There is an onion-service introduction component.

Pattern suggests network-wide or family-targeted, not host-specific.

Impact contained for their relays: DoS defenses engaged, zero TCP port exhaustion, zero global rate-limit events.

EU relays shed 10-20% of real traffic (closer to capacity). NA relays absorbed the load without shedding.

The symptom class matches previous DDoS attacks: 
- circuit creation floods overloading non-exit relays' 
- onionskin processing, plus an onion-service introduction component.

### Timeline (UTC)

Jun 22, 12:00-24:00: 12h precursor burst, open circuits ~8x normal, then two quiet days.

Jun 25, 23:00: onset. Onionskin processing ~2.5x within 30 minutes, open circuits ~6x within 3 hours.

Jun 26-27: first major waves. introduce2_rejected bursts an order of magnitude above normal (peak Jun 27 03:00). conn_rejected ~5x baseline, bursts to

~10x.

I don't have evidence that `#41339` is definitely caused by the same DoS, and I agree that it could still be a separate issue or a bug.
I linked it here because, when the repeated `Service descriptor has an invalid signature length. Expected 86 but got 88` messages occurred, they coincided with several of the same abnormal conditions being investigated in this issue.
In `#41339`, the original report also mentions unusually high circuit counts, DESTROY cells, BEGIN_DIR streams, ntor_v3 processing, ntor drops, congestion-control activity, high CPU usage, and RX >> TX. Other relay operators reported inbound saturation and memory pressure at the same time.
On my relay, the warning was repeated thousands of times around 16:04 on August 30. During that hour, RX increased from 34.63 GB in the previous hour to 150.36 GB, while TX remained at 38.33 GB, and the Tor process reached about 7.07 GiB RSS.
So I am not claiming that `#41339` has been proven to have the same root cause. My reason for linking it is the temporal correlation and the overlap in circuit, traffic, CPU, and memory symptoms. It seems possible that it is another vector or symptom of the broader DoS activity being investigated here, although a separate DoS or a bug cannot yet be ruled out.

passages:
A relay operator reports a sustained circuit-building DoS against their guard relay family, starting 2026-06-25 23:00 UTC and still ongoing as of 2026-07-10. 

Source: [tor-relays thread, "Abnormal Firewall-States since...", 10 Jul 2026.](https://lists.torproject.org/mailman3/hyperkitty/list/tor-relays@lists.torproject.org/thread/VCUWQJ7KECAOL5ADPFWGX5OMYPQJAWG3/)

## Observations as reported by the operator

Key signature: millions of near-idle circuits. Circuit and stream counts explode while bandwidth barely moves.

Reported deltas (Jun 25 - Jul 10 vs prior 15 days, fleet-wide via MetricsPort)

MetricChangeOpen circuits +719% (8x sustained, 20x at peak)

Onionskins processed+ 639% (7x)

Stream creation +1126% (12x)

Bandwidth +20%

All locations and providers (EU + NA) hit simultaneously with the same onset time.

Load arrives over existing OR connections: established TCP counts stayed flat.

There is an onion-service introduction component.

Pattern suggests network-wide or family-targeted, not host-specific.

Impact contained for their relays: DoS defenses engaged, zero TCP port exhaustion, zero global rate-limit events.

EU relays shed 10-20% of real traffic (closer to capacity). NA relays absorbed the load without shedding.

The symptom class matches previous DDoS attacks: 
- circuit creation floods overloading non-exit relays' 
- onionskin processing, plus an onion-service introduction component.

### Timeline (UTC)

Jun 22, 12:00-24:00: 12h precursor burst, open circuits ~8x normal, then two quiet days.

Jun 25, 23:00: onset. Onionskin processing ~2.5x within 30 minutes, open circuits ~6x within 3 hours.

Jun 26-27: first major waves. introduce2_rejected bursts an order of magnitude above normal (peak Jun 27 03:00). conn_rejected ~5x baseline, bursts to

~10x.

Jun 26-28: overload symptoms. Brief onionskin drops on a small subset of relays, OOM handler ~10x more active, Stable/Fast/Running flag counts dip ~5% (Guard -3%).

Jul 5, 08:00: peak, open circuits ~20x baseline.

Jul 6-10: slow decay, still ~5-6x baseline on Jul 10.

passages.author: mikeperry
passages.text:
@roypranto39 - it sounds like one of your guards could be experiencing a DoS attack? There is also a possibility that your services themselves are being connected to by clients specifying broken or slow rendezvous points (this could be an attack, but more likely is a consequence of network DoS conditions elsewhere).

In either case, setting the following torrc should change the behavior and at least prevent the issue from causing connectivity problems:

```code
LearnCircuitBuildTimeout 0
CircuitBuildTimeout 60
```

It would be useful to know if this does in fact address the connectivity issue for your services. If it solves the connectivity problem, it will rule out other potential causes.

Note that this will degrade performance of your service, so once we have a fix you should remove these lines.

We just released tor 0.4.9.16. This is mostly an emergency release aimed at
fixing a problem at the directory authority problem and thus only affects them.

Here is the announcement:
https://forum.torproject.org/t/security-release-0-4-9-16/22372

ChangeLog below:

Changes in version 0.4.9.16 - 2026-11-04
 This is an emergency release affecting only directory authorities. It
 includes fixes to address the thundering herd caused by the new required
 protover values introduced in the previous release.

 o Major features (authority):
 - Work around a bug where old clients did not, in fact, correctly
 handle unparseable microdescriptors in the way that we had hoped
 that they would. We triggered this bug by omitting TAP keys from
 microdescriptors. To solve this issue, instead of omitting TAP
 keys, we replace them with a dummy TAP key. (This is safe, because
 nothing has used TAP since v2 onion services.)
 - New consensus method 38 added for this TAP dummy key.

 from 3 to 2 which is causing <= 0.4.8.x clients to exit(1).

 - Regenerate fallback directories generated on November 04, 2026.

 o Minor bugfixes (dirauth):
 - Let dir auth fetches be twice as big, to allow for the fact that 9
 votes can exceed 16MB even compressed. Part of 41471; bugfix
 on 0.3.5.1-alpha.

David
