passages:
This is https://hackerone.com/reports/3931869

## Executive Summary

Alice, a Tor client operator, enables v3 onion-service client authorization and stores an x25519 private key in an owner-only `ClientOnionAuthDir`. If that file loses one Base32 character, Tor rejects the malformed credential but writes the remaining 51 key characters to a WARN log even when `SafeLogging` is set to its default value of `1`. Eve, a separate log reader who cannot read Alice's client-auth directory, can therefore obtain a near-complete private key from Tor's logs. This is not remotely triggerable, it does not expose a well-formed key, and the test did not connect to or decrypt an onion service.

| Field | Assessment |
| --- | --- |
| Asset | Tor core, v3 onion-service client authorization |
| Assessed release | Tor 0.4.9.11 |
| Earliest verified affected release | Tor 0.3.5.1-alpha |
| Fixed release | None identified; the statement is also present on the public `main` branch inspected on 2026-08-11 |
| Weakness | CWE-532, Insertion of Sensitive Information into Log File |
| Suggested severity | Low |

I reviewed the exact Tor 0.4.9.11 source, traced the relevant logging statement to its introducing change, checked the first feature release and current public branch, and reran the supplied PoC against the exact locally built binary. The run used a container with networking disabled, `DisableNetwork 1`, an owner-only auth directory, `SafeLogging 1`, and a dummy key. The malformed 51-character key appeared verbatim at WARN; a well-formed 52-character control key did not appear in the log.

The suggested Low severity reflects a real disclosure of secret key material with substantial prerequisites. An operator must enable the optional client-auth feature, a key file must be malformed in a spec

ific way, and a second principal must be able to read Tor's logs while being unable to read the auth directory. No cross-principal log access or successful descriptor decryption was demonstrated in the lab.

## Background

`ClientOnionAuthDir` is an opt-in Tor configuration setting. Each `.auth_private` file has four colon-separated fields:

```text
:descriptor:x25519:
```

In Tor 0.4.9.11, `hs_client_service_authorization_t.enc_seckey` is a Curve25519 secret key used to compute the decryption keys that let an authorized client decrypt an onion-service descriptor (`src/feature/hs/hs_client.h`, `hs_client_service_authorization_t`). Tor checks that `ClientOnionAuthDir` is private before enumerating it. On Unix-like systems, the directory helper creates private directories with mode `0700` and rejects inappropriate permissions unless a specifically permitted group mode applies (`src/lib/fs/dir.c`, `check_private_dir`).

Tor also documents `SafeLogging 1` as replacing all potentially sensitive strings, with an exception for messages more verbose than Notice. WARN is less verbose than Notice, so the documented exception does not apply here. `SafeLogging` defaults to `1` in `src/app/config/config.c`.

The relevant boundary is not between a remote user and Tor. It is between the principal that can read the client-auth directory and a lower-trust principal or system that can read logs. Tor supports stderr, stdout, syslog, file, controller, and API-backed logging. Tor-created file logs are opened with mode `0640`, but actual log readers, groups, collectors, support bundles, and retention rules are deployment-specific. The PoC captured stderr and did not establish that a particular production deployment exposes logs to another principal.

## Vulnerability Details

### Source-to-s

r branch, not this decoder-error branch. The second branch is included because it logs the same private-key field at the same severity for the same reason, but its practical recoverability depends on how the full-length input is malformed and was not measured here.

The parser later wipes `seckey_b32` before freeing it:

```c
if (seckey_b32) {
 memwipe(seckey_b32, 0, strlen(seckey_b32));
}
```

That cleanup protects the parser's in-memory copy after use, but it cannot remove the copy already emitted to a log destination.

### Release history

The length check and raw WARN interpolation were introduced by commit `3695ef63` on 2018-09-07. The change was titled `HSv3: Don't assert when reading bad client-side privkeys.` Its purpose was defensive input handling, but the new error path printed the rejected private-key field.

Tor 0.3.5.1-alpha is the earliest released snapshot I verified with the logging statement. Its ChangeLog identifies it as the first 0.3.5.x release and the release that added client authorization for v3 onion services. The earlier `tor-0.3.5.0-alpha-dev` snapshot did not contain this parser. I also verified the vulnerable statement in the assessed Tor 0.4.9.11 release and in the public `main` branch at commit `3bfb4986`, dated 2026-08-06. I did not inspect every intermediate patch tag individually, so I am not claiming that each intermediate release was separately confirmed. I found no public fixing change or fixed release for this exact sink.

### Public duplicate review

A read-only search of the public Tor issue tracker for client-auth private-key logging, `SafeLogging`, `.auth_private`, and the exact Base32 error wording did not locate an issue describing this source-to-sink path. Private HackerOne reports are not visible, so final duplicate status

remains unknown.

The closest public issue I found is [Tor issue 29135](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/29135), which reported that a failed client-auth connection logged an entire received onion-service descriptor at WARN. That issue concerns a different input, function, and sink. [Tor issue 29040](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/29040) concerns a crash caused by duplicate local credentials, and [Tor issue 27896](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/tor/-/work_items/27896) concerns Base32 padding acceptance. Neither describes disclosure of the local client-auth private-key field.

## Exploitability Analysis

The demonstrated primitive is narrow but concrete: a 51-character prefix of a 52-character Base32-encoded x25519 private key is copied from an owner-only credential file into a WARN log while safe logging is enabled.

For the exact truncation used in the PoC, enumerating all 32 possible final Base32 characters produces exactly two distinct 32-byte private keys. The original dummy key is one of those two values. The reduction from 32 suffix characters to two binary keys follows from the unused padding bits in the last Base32 character of a 32-byte value.

This does not establish universal key recovery. To turn the two candidates into a usable key, Eve would also need a way to associate the log line with the correct onion address and a reliable oracle. If Eve knows the onion address and can obtain the corresponding encrypted descriptor, attempting descriptor decryption with both candidates may distinguish the correct key. That chain was not executed, and no access to an onion service was demonstrated.

The complete practical prerequisites are:

1. Alice enables the optional `ClientOnionAuthDir` feature.
2. A correctly

structured `.auth_private` file contains a private key truncated to 51 Base32 characters. This can arise from operator or deployment-tool error; no remote trigger was identified.
3. Tor starts or otherwise reads that credential file with WARN messages directed to a log destination.
4. Eve can read that log destination or a copied support bundle, but cannot already read `ClientOnionAuthDir`.
5. For the conditional stronger impact, Eve can associate the logged prefix with an onion address and obtain a descriptor or another reliable check for the two candidate keys.

The positive runtime test fixed `SafeLogging` to `1`, used directory mode `0700` and file mode `0600`, supplied a 51-character dummy key, and observed the complete 51-character value in stderr at WARN. The negative control used the corresponding well-formed 52-character key under otherwise identical conditions and confirmed that it did not appear in stderr. Both Tor processes exited cleanly. Networking was disabled at both the container and Tor layers, which rules out a public service response as the source of the observed line.

Important limitations and counterevidence are:

- A well-formed key is not logged by this path.
- The malformed file is rejected, so Alice cannot use that file successfully until it is corrected.
- The trigger is local configuration state, not remote network input.
- If logs and the auth directory are readable only by the same principal, this finding creates no new principal boundary.
- The PoC did not verify syslog, a file log, a controller subscriber, a support workflow, descriptor decryption, or onion-service access.
- Deployment prevalence for `ClientOnionAuthDir` and cross-principal log access is unknown.

These constraints are why Low is more appropriate than Medium despite the

sensitivity of the field.

## Proof of Concept

The sibling `poc/poc.py` script is a bounded local reproducer. It creates temporary `0700` data and auth directories, writes only the included dummy fixture at mode `0600`, runs Tor with `DisableNetwork 1`, disables SocksPort and ORPort, captures stderr, terminates the exact process after startup, and removes the temporary directories. It runs both the malformed input and the well-formed negative control.

The preserved test used an exact Tor 0.4.9.11 binary with SHA-256:

```text
534c61c8f701a3052bb2be0986707a4234c341577cc1ad75abfa3dbb51a246ba
```

To reproduce safely, build the official `tor-0.4.9.11` tag in a disposable local environment, ensure that binary is selected as `tor`, block outbound networking at the container or VM layer, and run from this report directory:

```sh
cd poc
TOR_BINARY=tor POC_OUTPUT=result.json python3 poc.py
```

`TOR_BINARY` can instead name a report-relative executable. The script prints and optionally writes a JSON record containing the tested binary hash, permissions, configuration, matching log line, candidate count, negative-control result, and process exit codes.

The preserved run produced:

```json
{
 "auth_directory_mode": "0o700",
 "auth_file_mode": "0o600",
 "disable_network": true,
 "distinct_32_byte_keys_consistent_with_logged_prefix": 2,
 "input_key_length": 51,
 "matching_log_lines": [
 "Aug 11 05:40:58.000 [warn] Client authorization encoded base32 private key length is invalid: rcow3dfavmyanyqvhwnvnmfdqw34ydtrgv7jnelmqs4wi4uuxrc"
 ],
 "original_key_is_in_reconstructed_set": true,
 "safe_logging": 1,
 "schema": "tor-hs-client-auth-key-log-poc-v2",
 "secret_appears_in_stderr": true,
 "target_revision": "f3d28b2e0978ca075ec324834bec077673478ded",
 "tor_exit_code": 0,
 "tor_sha2

56": "534c61c8f701a3052bb2be0986707a4234c341577cc1ad75abfa3dbb51a246ba",
 "vulnerable": true,
 "well_formed_control_passed": tru

e,
 "well_formed_control_tor_exit_code": 0,
 "well_formed_key_appears_in_stderr": false
}
```

The logged value is the dummy fixture embedded in the PoC, not a production credential. The executed container used `--network none` and automatic removal; no test container remained after the run. The script removes its temporary credential and data directories. The intentionally preserved `result.json` remains beside the script for reviewer verification.

## Remediation

Private-key material should never be included in log messages, even when an operator disables `SafeLogging`. The most robust fix is to remove `seckey_b32` from both malformed-key warnings:

```c
if (strlen(seckey_b32) != BASE32_NOPAD_LEN(CURVE25519_SECKEY_LEN)) {
 log_warn(LD_REND, "Client authorization encoded base32 private key "
 "length is invalid");
 goto err;
}
```

Apply the same treatment to the Base32 decode failure. If diagnostic context is required, log only a safely handled filename or an error category, never the credential value. Passing the key through a SafeLogging helper would protect the default mode, but unconditional omission is preferable because `SafeLogging 0` should not turn private-key material into routine diagnostic output.

The existing `memwipe()` should remain. It is useful defense in depth for memory lifetime, although it cannot undo an earlier log write.

Add regression coverage to `src/test/test_hs_client.c` around `test_parse_auth_file_content()`:

1. Capture WARN output while parsing a 51-character key with `SafeLogging 1`; assert that the secret is absent.
2. Repeat with a full-length string containing an invalid Base32 character; assert that the supplied field is absent.
3. Repeat with `SafeLogging 0`; assert that private-key material is still absent.
4. Confirm that both

malformed values are rejected and still produce an actionable generic error.
5. Confirm that a valid 52-character key parses successfully without a WARN containing the key.

## Summary

Tor 0.4.9.11 copies a malformed v3 onion client-auth private-key field into WARN logs without applying SafeLogging redaction. The exact offline run showed that a one-character-truncated key is logged verbatim despite `SafeLogging 1`, reducing the dummy 32-byte key to exactly two candidates, while the valid-key control was not logged. The first verified affected release is 0.3.5.1-alpha, and the public `main` branch inspected on 2026-08-11 still contains the statement; no fixed release was identified.

The security consequence depends on a real separation between credential-file access and log access. No remote trigger, production log reader, descriptor decryption, or onion-service access was demonstrated, so the report is intentionally scoped as Low severity.

OpenAI Codex Security assisted with source review and report drafting. I manually verified the source-to-impact chain, scope, duplicate status, severity, and reproduced the behavior locally using the attached bounded, network-disabled PoC. No public Tor infrastructure or user data was accessed.

## Impact

A log reader who cannot access the owner-only ClientOnionAuthDir can receive 51 of 52 Base32 characters of a malformed x25519 client-auth private key from WARN output even with SafeLogging=1. The reproduced prefix reduced the 32-byte dummy key to exactly two candidates, which can materially undermine onion-service client authorization where log access is less trusted than credential-file access. The issue is local and configuration-dependent; no remote trigger, production key, or onion-service decryption was demonstrated.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text: But on the other hand... we use `DirTolerance::extend_lifetime` to declare that a directory can be used for 3 days after its Valid-After time. So although new clients wouldn't be able to bootstrap, existing clients would keep working for a while, and give us a bit of breathing room.

passages.author: nickm
passages.text:
> Hmmm. I do not like the idea of having a parser to succeed without any errors (excluding forward compatibility), yet returning incomplete data. That way, I fear that such bugs slip through without noticing, which could have quite a few privacy implications.

Hm. If we do it like that, I think we should at least warn on invalid RS entries. That would make sure that we noticed any bugs, without making the network unusable.

I don't think it would be as easy as you think to work around a bug like this: it wouldn't be just a matter of "a few hours" to fix it. 
The authorities would need to block whichever relays were doing the attack, and it isn't always easy to get all of them to take action on short notice. Then, the attacker could just try the attack from other relays, so we would need to fix arti (or upgrade all the authorities) on an emergency basis. And if the attacker is sensible, they would try doing their attack on a weekend, to slow us down... and for all that time, Arti clients wouldn't be able to use new consensuses.

passages.author: cve
passages.text:
> I don't quite know the base way to do this in the parse2 code. Do I define a wrapper for Protocols, or is there an option to override how the deftly macro acts?

The idea with parse2 is as follows: Every "basic" type that is parseable either implements `ItemArgumentParseable` (if it is a single argument) or `ItemValueParseable` (if it is an entire value, i.e. multiple arguments plus an optional object). Besides, the latter can also -- under certain circumstandes -- be derived using `derive_deftly`.

Certain types also implement `NormalItemArgument` instead of `ItemArgumentParseable` in the case that their `FromStr` and `Display` implementation matches their netdoc representation, in which case a blanket `ItemArgumentParseable` implementation will be provided based on that.

In this specific case, it seems that there is a [manual implementation](https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti/-/blob/main/crates/tor-netdoc/src/parse2/impls.rs?ref_type=heads#L92) of `ItemValueParseable` for `tor_protover::Protocols`, which you would also need to change if you don't plan on changing the canonical `FromStr` implementation.

> I am also thinking that we should make Arti's consensus parser tolerate and ignore bad routerstatus entries of a kind that C tor might generate, since otherwise we might hit other varieties of this vulnerability.

Hmmm. I do not like the idea of having a parser to succeed without any errors (excluding forward compatibility), yet returning incomplete data. That way, I fear that such bugs slip through without noticing, which could have quite a few privacy implications.

Right now, if someone would execute this attack, we would most likely immediately notice, block the malicious relays, and issue a directory authority fix.

Assuming, we would ignore invalid

passages.author: cve
passages.text: entries, Arti would silently discard these descriptors and malicious relay operators now have an opportunity to fingerprint clients, as they can now be sure that only CTor clients (or vice versa) are

passages:
Original title: Protover parser differential any relay operator can make the signed consensus unparseable for every Arti client

Reported via [HackerOne](https://hackerone.com/reports/3959033) not verified by me.

---

Arti parses protocol-version (`protover`) strings **strictly**, exactly as dir-spec defines them.
C tor parses them **leniently**. Because C tor is what directory authorities run, a relay operator
can publish a `proto` line that C tor accepts and Arti rejects. That string is copied verbatim into
the authority-signed consensus, and Arti's consensus parser treats one bad `pr` line as **fatal for
the entire document**.

One relay operator , no privileges, no key material, cost of one VPS , can therefore prevent
**every Arti client** from parsing the consensus, while C tor clients are entirely unaffected.

## The differential

Arti enforces the grammar:

```rust
// crates/tor-protover/src/lib.rs:579
fn is_good_number(n: &str) -> bool {
 n.chars().all(|ch| ch.is_ascii_digit()) && !n.starts_with('0')
}
```

and rejects repeated versions:

```rust
// crates/tor-protover/src/lib.rs:617
if (supported & mask) != 0 { return Err(ParseError::Duplicate); }
// crates/tor-protover/src/lib.rs:523
if (*foundmask & bit) != 0 { return Err(ParseError::Duplicate); }
```

C tor's `src/core/or/protover.c` uses `tor_parse_ulong()` (i.e. `strtoul`), which accepts leading
zeros, and its `parse_protocol_list()` performs **no duplicate detection at all** , it simply does
`out->bitmask |= bitmask_for_range(low, high);`.

Six spec-invalid tokens are accepted by C tor and rejected by Arti:

| Injected token | C tor `protover_list_is_invalid()` | Arti `Protocols::from_str` |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `Padding=007` | accept (= 7) | `Err(Malformed)` |
| `Padding=02` | accept (= 2) | `Err(Malfo

rmed)` |
| `Link=03-05` | accept (= 3-5) | `Err(Malformed)` |
| `Padding=2,2` | accept | `Err(Duplicate)` |
| `Padding=2 Padding=2` | accept | `Err(Duplicate)` |
| `Link=1-3,2` | accept | `Err(Duplicate)` |

Note that **Arti is the spec-correct implementation** here , dir-spec says
`Int = NON_ZERO_DIGIT / Int DIGIT`, "a decimal integer between 1 and 63 inclusive". That does not
help Arti, because the authorities run C tor.

## Taint path , verbatim propagation into a signed document

1. Attacker relay publishes `proto Padding=007` in its server descriptor.
2. C tor copies it **without validation**:
 `src/feature/dirparse/routerparse.c:839-841` → `router->protocol_list = tor_strdup(tok->args[0]);`
3. The only protover gate on the authority side accepts it:
 `src/feature/dirauth/dirvote.c:4747-4750` →
 `if (ri->protocol_list && protover_list_is_invalid(ri->protocol_list)) continue;`
 then copies it verbatim again at `dirvote.c:4779` → `vrs->protocols = tor_strdup(ri->protocol_list);`
4. Consensus computation selects and emits it verbatim:
 `dirvote.c:2160-2162` → `chosen_protocol_list = get_most_frequent_member(protocols);`
 `src/feature/nodelist/fmt_routerstatus.c:123-124` → `smartlist_add_asprintf(chunks, "pr %s\n", protocols);`
5. The token is now inside the **authority-signed** consensus. C tor clients are unaffected
 (`ns_parse.c:477-480` calls the same lenient check).
6. Arti rejects the routerstatus:
 
 ```rust
 // crates/tor-netdoc/src/doc/netstatus/rs/each_flavor.rs:143
 let tok = sec.required(RS_PR)?;
 tok.args_as_str().parse::().map_err(...)? // <-- Err
 ```
 
7. **And one bad entry aborts the whole document:**
 
 ```rust
 // crates/tor-netdoc/src/doc/netstatus/each_flavor.rs:189
 while let Some((pos, routerstatus)) = Self::take_routerstatus(r)? { // <-- `?` ab

orts
 ```
 
8. `tor-dirmgr` discards the consensus **before signature validation is reached**:
 
 ```rust
 // crates/tor-dirmgr/src/state.rs:361-363
 let (signedval, remainder, parsed) =
 MdConsensus::parse(text).map_err(|e| Error::from_netdoc(source.clone(), e))?;
 ```
 

Arti retries from a different directory cache , which serves the *same* authority-signed consensus ,
so the retry loop never converges. Consensus diffs do not help: the diff is applied and the result is
then parsed.

## Reproduction

From a fresh clone of `https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti`:

```bash
# crates/tor-netdoc/tests/ does not exist upstream and must be created
mkdir -p crates/tor-netdoc/tests
cp evidence/FIND-003/poc_pv_consensus.rs crates/tor-netdoc/tests/pv_consensus_poc.rs

cargo test -p tor-netdoc --test pv_consensus_poc -- --nocapture
```

The test injects each token into the real
`crates/tor-netdoc/testdata2/cached-microdesc-consensus` and parses it with the real
`MdConsensus::parse`:

```
inject `Padding=007` protover=Some(Malformed) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Padding=02` protover=Some(Malformed) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Link=03-05` protover=Some(Malformed) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Padding=2,2` protover=Some(Duplicate) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Padding=2 Padding=2` protover=Some(Duplicate) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1
inject `Link=1-3,2` protover=Some(Duplicate) whole-consensus=BROKEN: bad argument for entry on line 32, byte 1

test result: ok. 2 passed; 0 failed
```

A second test asserts the control direction , forms that C tor *also* rejects (`Pa

dding=0`,
`Padding=64`) are rejected by Arti too , confirming the differential is specific to the six tokens
above and not a blanket parser difference.

## Suggested remediation

Two independent fixes, either of which closes the outage; both are worth doing:

1. **Do not let one routerstatus destroy the document.** In
 `netstatus/each_flavor.rs:189`, treat a malformed `pr` line as "skip / degrade this relay"
 rather than propagating with `?`. A client that cannot parse one relay's protover can still use
 every other relay in the consensus. This also contains any *future* protover-grammar divergence.
2. **Align leniency with C tor for parsing** (while keeping the strict grammar for anything Arti
 *generates*): accept leading zeros and repeated versions on input. Arti is spec-correct today, but
 input parsing has to tolerate what the authorities actually sign.

Fix (1) is the important one , it removes the entire class, not just these six tokens.

## Impact

- **Fresh Arti clients can never bootstrap** for as long as the attacker's relay stays in the consensus.
- **Running clients** keep their cached consensus until it expires (hours), then can never replace it.
- The attacker sustains it simply by keeping the relay published.
- **C tor clients are entirely unaffected**, so the outage presents as an Arti-only failure , which
 makes it slower to diagnose.

This is the same class as the already-remediated TROVE-2026-24 / TROVE-2026-27 (malicious directory
input → Arti directory subsystem stops), reached through a different route.

passages.author: gabi-250
passages.text: I agree with your reasoning.

passages.author: opara
passages.text:
I don't see a way that this could be abused. If the client requested a loopback address (like if it loaded a page with a `src="http://[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:80/foo"` iframe) and the exit was malicious, the exit could "answer" as that loopback address. Some applications like browsers treat loopback addresses as special, but Firefox does not appear to for `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]`. Maybe the page loaded in that iframe could then make further requests against a loopback server that the user is running locally (since I think CORS would effectively be bypassed). But this is a lot of hypothesizing. **Edit:** This wouldn't make sense because those further requests against the loopback server would also go over Tor, not actual loopback. So I have nothing here.

So I think we can either make this public or make it "low-severity".

Reported via [HackerOne](https://hackerone.com/reports/3959006)

Relates to: https://gitlab.torproject.org/tpo/core/arti/-/work_items/2679

Original HackerOne title: `allow_local_addrs` does not treat IPv4-mapped IPv6 (and several other internal ranges) as local

---

# `allow_local_addrs` does not treat IPv4-mapped IPv6 (and several other internal ranges) as local
**Product:** Arti (Tor client) 
**Component:** `arti-client` address filter → SOCKS / HTTP CONNECT 
**Version tested:** 0.45.0 (current tree) 
**CWE:** CWE-180 (Incorrect Behavior Order: Validate Before Canonicalize) / CWE-200 (information exposure of stream target) 
**Weakness class:** Incomplete private-address classification before opening a Tor stream
---
## Summary
Arti’s default `address_filter.allow_local_addrs = false` is meant to refuse stream targets that “cannot meaningfully be connected to over Tor, and that the exit will not accept.” The check is `Host::is_local` in `crates/arti-client/src/address.rs`.
That function is incomplete:
| Target | Classified local today? | Should be (given the stated purpose)? |
|---|---|---|
| `127.0.0.1` | yes | yes |
| RFC1918 (`10/8`, `172.16/12`, `192.168/8`) | yes | yes |
| `::1` | yes | yes |
| `::ffff:127.0.0.1` / `::ffff:10.x.x.x` | **no** | yes (same hosts, IPv4-mapped) |
| `0.0.0.0` | **no** | yes (unspecified) |
| `169.254.0.0/16` | **no** | yes (IPv4 link-local) |
| `fc00::/7` (ULA) | **no** | yes |
| `fe80::/10` (IPv6 link-local) | **no** | yes |
| hostname `localhost` | yes | yes |
SOCKS and HTTP CONNECT both parse the application target into `TorAddr` and call `enforce_config`. Mapped and other missed addresses therefore **leave the client**, become a `BEGIN` at a chosen exit, and leak the intended destination into circuit construction. This is **not**

SSRF against the user’s own localhost (the TCP connection is still made by the exit). It **is** a broken local-address policy and a privacy leak relative to the documented filter.
---
## CVSS 3.1
**Vector:** `CVSS:3.1/AV:L/AC:L/PR:N/UI:N/S:U/C:L/I:N/A:N` 
**Base score:** **4.0 (Medium)**
| Metric | Value | Rationale |
|---|---|---|
| Attack Vector | Local | Needs a connection to Arti’s SOCKS/HTTP CONNECT port. Default listen is loopback. |
| Attack Complexity | Low | Send a normal proxy request with a mapped/internal literal. |
| Privileges Required | None | Any local process that can use the proxy. |
| User Interaction | None | |
| Scope | Unchanged | Affects this Arti instance’s stream policy / circuit use. |
| Confidentiality | Low | Destination that the user/policy intended to keep off-network is sent to the Tor network (guards/exit see a `BEGIN` for an internal-looking address). |
| Integrity | None | No write to the client host. |
| Availability | None | |
**Do not score this as client SSRF (C:H / S:C).** The client does not `connect()` to its own `127.0.0.1`. Ceiling impact if some exit *also* fails to reject mapped-loopback is access to **that exit’s** loopback, which is an exit-policy issue on top of this client bug and is **not assumed** here.
If SOCKS is deliberately bound on a non-loopback address (Arti already warns this is insecure), AV becomes Network and the score rises (`AV:N` → **5.3** with the same other metrics). That is a deployment choice, not the default.
---
## Reachability
**In scope / reachable on a default Arti proxy**
1. Arti running as a SOCKS (and/or HTTP CONNECT) proxy with default `allow_local_addrs = false`.
2. A local application (or anything that can open TCP to the proxy) issues `CONNECT` to a missed address form.
3. `Host::from_str`

/ `SocketAddr::from_str` accepts the literal as `Host::Ip`.
4. `enforce_config` does **not** return `ErrorDetail::LocalAddress`.
5. `TorClient::connect_with_prefs` builds a circuit and sends `BEGIN`.
**Call chain (SOCKS):** 
`arti/src/proxy/socks.rs` `handle_socks_conn` → `(addr, port).into_tor_addr()` → `connect_with_prefs` → `into_stream_instructions` → `enforce_config` → `Host::is_local`.
**Call chain (HTTP CONNECT):** 
`arti/src/proxy/http_connect.rs` `handle_connect_request_impl` → `TorAddr::from(&target)` → same `connect_with_prefs` path.
**Not required:** RPC, onion services, `allow_local_addrs = true`, non-loopback SOCKS bind.
**Not claimed:** Remote website → Arti. Browsers do not issue SOCKS without a configured proxy; HTTP CONNECT to Arti from a remote `Host` is separately blocked for non-CONNECT methods. This is a **local proxy policy** bug.
---
## Technical details
```443:455:crates/arti-client/src/address.rs
 fn is_local(&self) -> bool {
 match self {
 Host::Hostname(name) => name.eq_ignore_ascii_case("localhost"),
 Host::Ip(IpAddr::V4(ip)) => ip.is_loopback() || ip.is_private(),
 Host::Ip(IpAddr::V6(ip)) => ip.is_loopback(),
 Host::Onion(_) => false,
 }
 }
```
Rust `Ipv6Addr::is_loopback()` is **only** `::1/128`. IPv4-mapped addresses (`::ffff:0:0/96`) are **not** loopback, even when the embedded v4 address is `127.0.0.1`. `Ipv4Addr::is_private()` is RFC1918 only (not unspecified, not link-local). The IPv6 arm never calls `is_unique_local`, `is_unicast_link_local`, or `to_ipv4_mapped()`.
The comment on this function states the purpose is to catch addresses exits will not accept. The relay-side helper `ChanTarget::all_addrs_allowed_for_outgoing_channels` already treats unspecified, RFC1918, v4 link-local, ULA, and v6 link-local as disallowed for **native**

forms — but the client filter does not match that set, and **neither** helper unwraps mapped IPv4.
SOCKS5 `ATYP=4` with a mapped address, or a URI `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:port`, both become `Host::Ip(V6)`. `Begin` encoding then sends that IPv6 literal to the exit.
---
## Steps to reproduce (for triagers)
No network attack is required. In-tree unit test style:
```rust
// default ClientAddrConfig: allow_local_addrs = false
assert!(matches!(
 TorAddr::from("127.0.0.1:80")?.enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs),
 Err(ErrorDetail::LocalAddress)
));
// current tree: these succeed (the bug)
assert!(TorAddr::from("[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
assert!(TorAddr::from("[::ffff:10.1.2.3]:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
assert!(TorAddr::from("0.0.0.0:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
assert!(TorAddr::from("169.254.1.1:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
assert!(TorAddr::from("[fd12:3456::1]:80")
 .unwrap()
 .enforce_config(&Default::default(), &prefs)
 .is_ok());
```
Optional live check (local Arti only): SOCKS CONNECT to `[::ffff:127.0.0.1]:80` with default config. Observe that Arti does **not** fail fast with “local address”; it attempts a circuit. Do **not** scan third-party exits.
---
## Impact
1. **Policy bypass.** Applications and users who rely on `allow_local_addrs = false` (the default) can still request internal-looking destinations via mapped IPv6 or the missed ranges.
2. **Privacy / traffic confirmation.** A local app can force circuit use and a `BEGIN` for addresses the client intended never to emit. Guards and the exit observe that attempt.
3. **Exit interaction (unclaimed extra).** If

an exit’s policy also fails to reject mapped-loopback, the stream would land on the **exit’s** loopback. That is out of Arti’s hands; C-tor generally rejects internal destinations after mapping. Do not treat this report as “RCE on exits.”
**Non-impacts:** no deanonymization of the client’s IP beyond normal Tor use; no read of the client’s local services; no crypto break.
---
## Remediation
In `Host::is_local` (and keep SOCKS/HTTP on `enforce_config`):
1. If IPv6, `to_ipv4_mapped()` and classify the embedded v4 with the **same** v4 rules.
2. IPv4: also `is_unspecified()`, `is_link_local()` (and consider `0.0.0.0/8` if you want C-tor parity).
3. IPv6: `is_unique_local()`, `is_unicast_link_local()`, `is_unspecified()`, multicast as needed.
4. Prefer a shared helper with `all_addrs_allowed_for_outgoing_channels` so client and relay cannot drift.
5. Add regression tests for the table in the summary (including mapped loopback and mapped RFC1918).
6. Existing tests in `local_addrs()` only cover `localhost`, `127.0.0.1`, `::1`, `192.168.0.1`.
`is_global()` (once stable) is a reasonable long-term target; the comment already mentions it.
---
## Related
- Same crate comment points at a different helper (`tor-hsrproxy` `is_sufficiently_private`) and issue #1159. Mapped IPv6 is **not** covered by the existing `is_local` tests even if #1159 is known for other gaps.
- Sister issue: relay EXTEND2 mapped-IPv6 check in `tor-linkspec` (separate HackerOne report).

## Impact

## Impact
1. **Policy bypass.** Applications and users who rely on `allow_local_addrs = false` (the default) can still request internal-looking destinations via mapped IPv6 or the missed ranges.
2. **Privacy / traffic confirmation.** A local app can force circuit use and a `BEGIN` for addresses the client intended nev

er to emit. Guards and the exit observe that attempt.
3. **Exit interaction (unclaimed extra).** If an exit’s policy also fails to reject mapped-loopback, the stream would land on the **exit’s** loopback. That is out of Arti’s hands; C-tor generally rejects internal destinations after mapping. Do not treat this report as “RCE on exits.”
**Non-impacts:** no deanonymization of the client’s IP beyond normal Tor use; no read of the client’s local services; no crypto break.

candidate.title: Arti reported to have proof-of-work queue bypass allowing zero-effort eviction
candidate.summary: A security report filed via HackerOne and published on GitLab describes a defect in Arti's rendezvous queue where a client sending no proof-of-work can evict a queued client that did. The defect requires the non-default enable_pow setting and the experimental hs-pow-full feature. The report states this defeats the priority queue's purpose but notes it does not demonstrate a sustained denial of service. A maintainer commented that the issue is a bug but does not seem like a DoS issue, and a fix issue was created.

unsupported: A client that performs no proof-of-work can evict a queued client that did, defeating the purpose of the priority queue.

candidate.title: Tor patch fixes bug where clients permanently shun exits after transient errors
candidate.summary: A bug in Tor's nodelist handling caused clients to permanently mark an exit relay as rejecting all traffic after receiving a single transient RELAY_END message, such as RESOURCELIMIT or HIBERNATING. This issue, introduced in Tor 0.2.3.1-alpha, allowed a third party to steer clients away from honest exits by exhausting an exit's sockets or sending a malicious END, though a maintainer said it is hard to turn into a targeted security attack. The fix clears the 'rejects_all' flag when a new consensus is installed.

unsupported: Tor Browser users and other long-running clients will receive the fix in the next stable release.

We will continue without this key, but this may prevent clients from connecting..." The user asks whether something they did corrupted the on-disk PoW state or whether a code change causes the warning.

prior_story.title: Tor 0.4.9.15 security release adds DoS defenses and drops 0.4.8 support
prior_story.summary: The Tor Project released version 0.4.9.15 with new defenses against large volumes of directory requests and an HSDir flag that persists across restarts. Its announcement said new required protocol capabilities would make Tor 0.4.8 and earlier unable to use the network, and asked relay operators to upgrade as soon as possible.
prior_story.why_it_matters: The announcement describes new protections against excessive directory requests and changes to directory-authority protocol requirements.

prior_story.title: Operator reports circuit-building DoS against guard relays in June–July 2026
prior_story.summary: An operator reported a circuit-building DoS against its guard-relay family beginning June 25, 2026 and still ongoing as of July 10. The report describes open circuits at roughly 8x baseline during sustained load and 20x at peak, with bandwidth up 20%; its timeline records a decline to about 5–6x baseline by July 10. The operator said defenses engaged without TCP-port exhaustion, while EU relays shed 10–20% of real traffic.
prior_story.why_it_matters: The report suggests the pattern is network-wide or family-targeted, and notes that EU relays shed 10-20% of real traffic.

prior_story.title: Tor authority bastet to be removed from source after reported compromise
prior_story.summary: The Tor development team reported that the operator of the bastet directory authority notified them that the machine is very plausibly compromised. The report states that bastet will be removed from the source code because its keys can no longer be trusted. The operator is expected to generate a new identity for the authority.
prior_story.why_it_matters: The report says bastet's existing keys can no longer be trusted and requests removal of its current entry from the software.
